name: code-review
description: Review code for bugs, security vulnerabilities, performance issues, and maintainability. Trigger with "review this code", "check this PR", "look at this diff", "is this code safe?", or when the user shares code and asks for feedback.
---

# Code Review

Structured code review covering security, performance, correctness, and maintainability. Works on diffs, PRs, files, or pasted code snippets.

## Review Dimensions

### Security
- SQL injection, XSS, CSRF
- Authentication and authorization flaws
- Secrets or credentials in code
- Insecure deserialization
- Path traversal
- SSRF

### Performance
- N+1 queries
- Unnecessary memory allocations
- Algorithmic complexity (O(n²) in hot paths)
- Missing database indexes
- Unbounded queries or loops
- Resource leaks

### Correctness
- Edge cases (empty input, null, overflow)
- Race conditions and concurrency issues
- Error handling and propagation
- Off-by-one errors
- Type safety

### Maintainability
- Naming clarity
- Single responsibility
- Duplication
- Test coverage
- Documentation for non-obvious logic

## Output Format

Rate each dimension and provide specific, actionable findings with file and line references. Prioritize critical issues first. Always include positive observations alongside issues.

     1	// Six pillars as nodes with the dependency arcs of the Formalized State (Part VII):
     2	// production feeds every other function; allocation feeds production; the other four feed allocation.
     3	const NODES = [
     4	  { id: 'F', label: 'Financial', x: 300, y: 250, color: '#d9b25f' },
     5	  { id: 'W', label: 'Productive', x: 300, y: 450, color: '#4fb286' },
     6	  { id: 'P', label: 'Political', x: 62, y: 210, color: '#e0556a' },
     7	  { id: 'J', label: 'Judicial', x: 538, y: 210, color: '#6f8fe0' },
     8	  { id: 'I', label: 'Ideological', x: 160, y: 62, color: '#b072d8' },
     9	  { id: 'C', label: 'Coercive', x: 440, y: 62, color: '#e8793a' },
    10	];
    11	
    12	const R = 30;
    13	const pos = Object.fromEntries(NODES.map((n) => [n.id, n]));
    14	
    15	function arc(a: string, b: string, bend: number) {
    16	  const A = pos[a];
    17	  const B = pos[b];
    18	  const dx = B.x - A.x;
    19	  const dy = B.y - A.y;
    20	  const d = Math.hypot(dx, dy);
    21	  const ux = dx / d;
    22	  const uy = dy / d;
    23	  const sx = A.x + ux * (R + 2);
    24	  const sy = A.y + uy * (R + 2);
    25	  const ex = B.x - ux * (R + 8);
    26	  const ey = B.y - uy * (R + 8);
    27	  const mx = (sx + ex) / 2 - uy * bend;
    28	  const my = (sy + ey) / 2 + ux * bend;
    29	  return `M${sx.toFixed(1)} ${sy.toFixed(1)} Q${mx.toFixed(1)} ${my.toFixed(1)} ${ex.toFixed(1)} ${ey.toFixed(1)}`;
    30	}
    31

    35	  ['W', 'I', -95],

    37	] as const;
    38	const INTO_F = [

    40	  ['J', 'F', 0],
    41	  ['I', 'F', 0],
    42	  ['C', 'F', 0],
    43	] as const;

Financial power feeds productive power, and the political, judicial, ideological and coercive pillars each feed financial power."
    52	      >
    53	        <defs>
    54	          <marker id="arrow-solid" viewBox="0 0 10 10" refX="8" refY="5" markerWidth="7" markerHeight="7" orient="auto-start-reverse">
    55	            <path d="M0 0L10 5L0 10z" fill="#ec5a72" />
    56	          </marker>
    57	          <marker id="arrow-soft" viewBox="0 0 10 10" refX="8" refY="5" markerWidth="6" markerHeight="6" orient="auto-start-reverse">

    66	        <g fill="none" strokeLinecap="round">
    67	          {FROM_W.map(([a, b, bend]) => (
    68	            <path key={a + b} d={arc(a, b, bend)} stroke="#8d867b" strokeWidth="1.5" strokeDasharray="5 4" markerEnd="url(#arrow-soft)" />

    76	        {NODES.map((n) => (

    85	              textAnchor={n.id === 'F' ? 'start' : 'middle'}

     1	'use client';
     2	import { useEffect, useState } from 'react';
     3	
     4	export type Heading = { id: string; text: string; level: number };
     5	
     6	export function TableOfContents({ headings }: { headings: Heading[] }) {
     7	  const [activeId, setActiveId] = useState('');
     8	  const [open, setOpen] = useState(false);
     9	
    10	  useEffect(() => {
    11	    const onScroll = () => {
    12	      const scrollY = window.scrollY + 100;
    13	      let current = '';
    14	      for (const { id } of headings) {
    15	        const el = document.getElementById(id);
    16	        if (el && el.getBoundingClientRect().top + window.scrollY <= scrollY) current = id;
    17	      }
    18	      setActiveId(current);
    19	    };
    20	    window.addEventListener('scroll', onScroll, { passive: true });
    21	    window.addEventListener('resize', onScroll);
    22	    const t = window.setTimeout(onScroll, 50); // content is injected after mount
    23	    onScroll();
    24	    return () => {
    25	      window.removeEventListener('scroll', onScroll);
    26	      window.removeEventListener('resize', onScroll);
    27	      window.clearTimeout(t);
    28	    };
    29	  }, [headings]);
    30	
    31	  return (
    32	    <div className={`toc-wrap ${open ? 'toc-open' : ''}`}>
    33	      <button
    34	        type="button"
    35	        className="toc-toggle"
    36	        aria-expanded={open}
    37	        aria-controls="toc-panel"
    38	        onClick={() => setOpen((o) => !o)}
    39	      >
    40	        <span>Contents</span>
    41	        <span className="burger" aria-hidden="true">
    42	          <i />
    43	          <i />
    44	          <i />
    45	        </span>
    46	      </button>
    47	      <nav className="toc-panel" id="toc-panel" aria-label="Table of contents">
    48	        <p className="toc-title">Contents</p>
    49	        {headings.map(({ id, text, level }) => (
    50	          <a
    51	            key={id}
    52	            href={`#${id}`}
    53	            onClick={() => setOpen(false)}
    54	            className={`toc-item ${level === 3 ? 'toc-sub' : ''} ${activeId === id ? 'toc-active' : ''}`}
    55	            aria-current={activeId === id ? 'location' : undefined}
    56	          >
    57	            {text}
    58	          </a>
    59	        ))}
    60	      </nav>
    61	    </div>
    62	  );
    63	}

FILE website/lib/render-math.ts
     1	// Build-time math: replaces LaTeX delimiters in an HTML string with KaTeX markup.
     2	import katex from 'katex';
     3	import extracted from './macros.json';
     4	
     5	// Macros extracted from the \newcommand / \DeclareMathOperator lines of all seven preambles
     6	// (scripts/extract-macros.mjs), plus a few notation helpers.
     7	export const MACROS: Record<string, string> = {
     8	  '\\slashed': '\\not{#1}',
     9	  '\\bra': '\\langle #1|',
    10	  '\\ket': '|#1\\rangle',
    11	  '\\braket': '\\langle #1\\rangle',
    12	  '\\Hom': '\\operatorname{Hom}',
    13	  '\\Tr': '\\operatorname{Tr}',
    14	  '\\Lan': '\\operatorname{Lan}',
    15	  '\\Ran': '\\operatorname{Ran}',
    16	  ...(extracted as Record<string, string>),
    17	};
    18	
    19	function unescapeHtml(s: string) {
    20	  return s
    21	    .replace(/&lt;/g, '<')
    22	    .replace(/&gt;/g, '>')
    23	    .replace(/&quot;/g, '"')
    24	    .replace(/&#39;/g, "'")
    25	    .replace(/&amp;/g, '&');
    26	}
    27	
    28	function render(tex: string, displayMode: boolean) {
    29	  return katex.renderToString(tex, {
    30	    displayMode,
    31	    throwOnError: false,
    32	    trust: true,
    33	    strict: 'ignore',
    34	    macros: { ...MACROS },
    35	  });
    36	}
    37	
    38	export function renderMath(html: string): string {
    39	  // pandoc output: <span class="math inline">\( ... \)</span>
    40	  let out = html.replace(
    41	    /<span class="math (inline|display)">\\[(\[]([\s\S]*?)\\[)\]]<\/span>/g,
    42	    (_, kind: string, tex: string) => {
    43	      const display = kind === 'display';
    44	      const rendered = render(unescapeHtml(tex), display);
    45	      return display ? `<div class="math-display">${rendered}</div>` : rendered;
    46	    },
    47	  );
    48	  // any remaining bare delimiters
    49	  out = out.replace(/\$\$([\s\S]+?)\$\$/g, (_, t: string) => render(unescapeHtml(t), true));
    50	  out = out.replace(/\\\[([\s\S]+?)\\\]/g, (_, t: string) => render(unescapeHtml(t), true));
    51	  out = out.replace(/\\\(([\s\S]+?)\\\)/g, (_, t: string) => render(unescapeHtml(t), false));
    52	  return out;
    53	}

FILE website/scripts/extract-macros.mjs
     1	// Step 2: collect every \newcommand, \renewcommand and \DeclareMathOperator from the paper preambles
     2	// into website/lib/macros.json (KaTeX macro map).
     3	import fs from 'node:fs';
     4	import path from 'node:path';
     5	import { SLUGS } from './series.mjs';
     6	
     7	const root = path.resolve(process.argv[2] || '.');
     8	const macros = {};
     9	const seen = {};
    10	const conflicts = [];
    11	
    12	function group(s, i) {
    13	  let d = 0;
    14	  for (let j = i; j < s.length; j++) {
    15	    if (s[j] === '\\') { j++; continue; }
    16	    if (s[j] === '{') d++;
    17	    else if (s[j] === '}' && --d === 0) return j;
    18	  }
    19	  throw new Error('unbalanced');
    20	}
    21	
    22	for (const slug of SLUGS) {
    23	  const tex = fs.readFileSync(path.join(root, 'papers', 'latex', `${slug}.tex`), 'utf8');
    24	  const pre = tex.slice(0, tex.indexOf('\\begin{document}'));
    25	  const re = /\\(newcommand|renewcommand|providecommand|DeclareMathOperator)(\*?)\s*\{?(\\[A-Za-z]+)\}?(\[\d\])?\s*\{/g;
    26	  let m;
    27	  while ((m = re.exec(pre))) {
    28	    const [, kind, star, name, nargs] = m;
    29	    const start = m.index + m[0].length - 1;
    30	    const end = group(pre, start);
    31	    let body = pre.slice(start + 1, end).trim();
    32	    if (kind === 'DeclareMathOperator') body = `\\operatorname${star}{${body}}`;
    33	    (seen[name] ||= new Set()).add(body);
    34	    if (!(name in macros)) macros[name] = body;
    35	    else if (macros[name] !== body) conflicts.push(`${name} (${slug}): ${body} vs ${macros[name]}`);
    36	  }
    37	}
    38	const out = Object.fromEntries(Object.entries(macros).sort());
    39	fs.writeFileSync(path.join(root, 'website', 'lib', 'macros.json'), JSON.stringify(out, null, 2) + '\n');
    40	console.log(`macros: ${Object.keys(out).length} unique names (${conflicts.length} cross-paper redefinitions)`);

    29	function matchBrace(s, i) {
    30	  // s[i] === '{'; return index of the matching '}'
    31	  let d = 0;
    32	  for (let j = i; j < s.length; j++) {
    33	    if (s[j] === '\\') { j++; continue; }
    34	    if (s[j] === '{') d++;
    35	    else if (s[j] === '}') { d--; if (d === 0) return j; }
    36	  }
    37	  throw new Error('unbalanced brace');
    38	}

    40	function countCols(spec) {
    41	  let n = 0;
    42	  for (let i = 0; i < spec.length; i++) {
    43	    const c = spec[i];
    44	    if (c === '@' || c === '>' || c === '<' || c === '!') { i = matchBrace(spec, i + 1); continue; }
    45	    if ('LpmbCPR'.includes(c)) { n++; if (spec[i + 1] === '{') i = matchBrace(spec, i + 1); continue; }
    46	    if ('lcrYX'.includes(c)) n++;
    47	  }
    48	  return n;
    49	}

    51	function fixTabularx(tex) {
    52	  let out = '';
    53	  let i = 0;
    54	  const tag = '\\begin{tabularx}';
    55	  while (true) {
    56	    const k = tex.indexOf(tag, i);
    57	    if (k < 0) { out += tex.slice(i); break; }
    58	    out += tex.slice(i, k);
    59	    let p = k + tag.length;
    60	    const wEnd = matchBrace(tex, p); // width arg
    61	    p = wEnd + 1;
    62	    const sEnd = matchBrace(tex, p);
    63	    const spec = tex.slice(p + 1, sEnd);
    64	    out += `\\begin{tabular}{${'l'.repeat(countCols(spec))}}`;
    65	    i = sEnd + 1;
    66	  }
    67	  return out.replaceAll('\\end{tabularx}', '\\end{tabular}');
    68	}

     1	// Build-time math: replaces LaTeX delimiters in an HTML string with KaTeX markup.
     2	import katex from 'katex';
     3	import extracted from './macros.json';
     4	
     5	// Macros extracted from the \newcommand / \DeclareMathOperator lines of all seven preambles
     6	// (scripts/extract-macros.mjs), plus a few notation helpers.
     7	export const MACROS: Record<string, string> = {
     8	  '\\slashed': '\\not{#1}',
     9	  '\\bra': '\\langle #1|',
    10	  '\\ket': '|#1\\rangle',
    11	  '\\braket': '\\langle #1\\rangle',
    12	  '\\Hom': '\\operatorname{Hom}',
    13	  '\\Tr': '\\operatorname{Tr}',
    14	  '\\Lan': '\\operatorname{Lan}',
    15	  '\\Ran': '\\operatorname{Ran}',
    16	  ...(extracted as Record<string, string>),
    17	};
    18	
    19	function unescapeHtml(s: string) {
    20	  return s
    21	    .replace(/&lt;/g, '<')
    22	    .replace(/&gt;/g, '>')
    23	    .replace(/&quot;/g, '"')
    24	    .replace(/&#39;/g, "'")
    25	    .replace(/&amp;/g, '&');
    26	}
    27	
    28	function render(tex: string, displayMode: boolean) {
    29	  return katex.renderToString(tex, {
    30	    displayMode,
    31	    throwOnError: false,
    32	    trust: true,
    33	    strict: 'ignore',
    34	    macros: { ...MACROS },
    35	  });
    36	}
    37	
    38	export function renderMath(html: string): string {
    39	  // pandoc output: <span class="math inline">\( ... \)</span>
    40	  let out = html.replace(
    41	    /<span class="math (inline|display)">\\[(\[]([\s\S]*?)\\[)\]]<\/span>/g,
    42	    (_, kind: string, tex: string) => {
    43	      const display = kind === 'display';
    44	      const rendered = render(unescapeHtml(tex), display);
    45	      return display ? `<div class="math-display">${rendered}</div>` : rendered;
    46	    },
    47	  );
    48	  // any remaining bare delimiters
    49	  out = out.replace(/\$\$([\s\S]+?)\$\$/g, (_, t: string) => render(unescapeHtml(t), true));
    50	  out = out.replace(/\\\[([\s\S]+?)\\\]/g, (_, t: string) => render(unescapeHtml(t), true));
    51	  out = out.replace(/\\\(([\s\S]+?)\\\)/g, (_, t: string) => render(unescapeHtml(t), false));
    52	  return out;
    53	}

     1	// Step 2: collect every \newcommand, \renewcommand and \DeclareMathOperator from the paper preambles
     2	// into website/lib/macros.json (KaTeX macro map).
     3	import fs from 'node:fs';
     4	import path from 'node:path';
     5	import { SLUGS } from './series.mjs';
     6	
     7	const root = path.resolve(process.argv[2] || '.');
     8	const macros = {};
     9	const seen = {};
    10	const conflicts = [];
    11	
    12	function group(s, i) {
    13	  let d = 0;
    14	  for (let j = i; j < s.length; j++) {
    15	    if (s[j] === '\\') { j++; continue; }
    16	    if (s[j] === '{') d++;
    17	    else if (s[j] === '}' && --d === 0) return j;
    18	  }
    19	  throw new Error('unbalanced');
    20	}
    21	
    22	for (const slug of SLUGS) {
    23	  const tex = fs.readFileSync(path.join(root, 'papers', 'latex', `${slug}.tex`), 'utf8');
    24	  const pre = tex.slice(0, tex.indexOf('\\begin{document}'));
    25	  const re = /\\(newcommand|renewcommand|providecommand|DeclareMathOperator)(\*?)\s*\{?(\\[A-Za-z]+)\}?(\[\d\])?\s*\{/g;
    26	  let m;
    27	  while ((m = re.exec(pre))) {
    28	    const [, kind, star, name, nargs] = m;
    29	    const start = m.index + m[0].length - 1;
    30	    const end = group(pre, start);
    31	    let body = pre.slice(start + 1, end).trim();
    32	    if (kind === 'DeclareMathOperator') body = `\\operatorname${star}{${body}}`;
    33	    (seen[name] ||= new Set()).add(body);
    34	    if (!(name in macros)) macros[name] = body;
    35	    else if (macros[name] !== body) conflicts.push(`${name} (${slug}): ${body} vs ${macros[name]}`);
    36	  }
    37	}
    38	const out = Object.fromEntries(Object.entries(macros).sort());
    39	fs.writeFileSync(path.join(root, 'website', 'lib', 'macros.json'), JSON.stringify(out, null, 2) + '\n');

     1	// Six pillars as nodes with the dependency arcs of the Formalized State (Part VII):
     2	// production feeds every other function; allocation feeds production; the other four feed allocation.
     3	const NODES = [
     4	  { id: 'F', label: 'Financial', x: 300, y: 250, color: '#d9b25f' },
     5	  { id: 'W', label: 'Productive', x: 300, y: 450, color: '#4fb286' },
     6	  { id: 'P', label: 'Political', x: 62, y: 210, color: '#e0556a' },
     7	  { id: 'J', label: 'Judicial', x: 538, y: 210, color: '#6f8fe0' },
     8	  { id: 'I', label: 'Ideological', x: 160, y: 62, color: '#b072d8' },
     9	  { id: 'C', label: 'Coercive', x: 440, y: 62, color: '#e8793a' },
    10	];
    11	
    12	const R = 30;
    13	const pos = Object.fromEntries(NODES.map((n) => [n.id, n]));
    14	
    15	function arc(a: string, b: string, bend: number) {
    16	  const A = pos[a];
    17	  const B = pos[b];
    18	  const dx = B.x - A.x;
    19	  const dy = B.y - A.y;
    20	  const d = Math.hypot(dx, dy);
    21	  const ux = dx / d;
    22	  const uy = dy / d;
    23	  const sx = A.x + ux * (R + 2);
    24	  const sy = A.y + uy * (R + 2);
    25	  const ex = B.x - ux * (R + 8);
    26	  const ey = B.y - uy * (R + 8);
    27	  const mx = (sx + ex) / 2 - uy * bend;
    28	  const my = (sy + ey) / 2 + ux * bend;
    29	  return `M${sx.toFixed(1)} ${sy.toFixed(1)} Q${mx.toFixed(1)} ${my.toFixed(1)} ${ex.toFixed(1)} ${ey.toFixed(1)}`;
    30	}

website/out/papers/financial-power/index.txt:160:<p>The economic theory of regulation asks how resource holders shape the rules that govern them. Stigler’s theory of economic regulation treats regulation as a good demanded by industries and supplied by the state, so that regulatory agencies tend to serve the regulated (Stigler 1971). Peltzman generalized the model: a regulator balances producer and consumer pressure, so outcomes fall between pure capture and pure public interest (Peltzman 1976). Becker showed that competition among pressure groups limits the transfers any one group can extract, because deadweight losses grow with the size of the transfer and mobilize the losers (Becker 1983). Laffont and Tirole recast capture as a principal-supervisor-agent problem in which the danger of collusion between the supervisor and the regulated firm shapes the optimal design of incentives (Laffont and Tirole 1991). Grossman and Helpman modeled trade protection as the outcome of contribution schedules offered to an incumbent government (Grossman and Helpman 1994). Dal Bó surveys the theory and evidence (Dal Bó 2006), and Carpenter and Moss insist on a demanding definition: capture requires showing that regulation was directed away from the public interest and toward the regulated industry by the industry’s own intent and action, not merely that the industry benefited (Carpenter and Moss 2014). That standard is the same one the capture link of Largo (2026) encodes.</p>
website/out/papers/financial-power/index.txt:177:<p>Formal concentration overstates effective concentration. Gregory’s study of the Soviet archives shows that the top leadership could not allocate everything and bargained constantly with ministries and enterprises that held better information about their own capacities (Gregory 2004). Berliner’s interviews with former Soviet managers documented the informal procurement agents who obtained scarce inputs outside the plan, and the networks of favors through which managers met targets (Berliner 1957); Ledeneva reconstructed the economy of favors, known as blat, that ran alongside the formal allocation of goods in the late Soviet period (Ledeneva 1998). These informal channels lowered effective concentration while also lowering contestability, since favors were by nature unrecorded and unreviewable. Kornai’s soft budget constraint completes the picture: enterprises expected rescue from their administrative superiors, so loss did not lead to exit, and the allocation of credit followed bargaining power rather than performance (Kornai 1986).</p>
website/out/papers/coercive-power/index.txt:5:2:T641,Every governance system must decide who enforces its rules. This paper derives the coercive function from one axiom, that members sometimes have reason to break rules, and compares how six regime types distribute it. A deterrence theorem shows that when the share of agents tempted to violate a rule exceeds the violation rate the collective can tolerate, compliance requires that violators’ continuation payoffs fall because of their own conduct. A sanction regime of some kind is therefore necessary, but no particular institution is. Gossip, ostracism and coalition action against would-be dominants meet this requirement as well as police do, as the ethnography of the Nuer, the Ju/’hoansi, Amazonian societies and Ostrom’s commons documents. A second result shows why, where sanctions are costly public goods and higher-order sanctions are absent, coercion at scale depends on provisioning or on shared norms of punishment. The paper then separates two properties of any enforcement apparatus: its conduct margin, how much more likely a violator is to be sanctioned than a complier, and its allegiance margin, how much more likely an opponent is to be sanctioned than a supporter. The two margins vary independently, so the necessity of coercion does not imply its capture. When capacity is limited, allegiance targeting weakens deterrence for at least one group; when opponents are targeted regardless of conduct, it also raises the volume of coercion against them, so spending and arrest counts mismeasure coercive power. The main limitation is that neither margin has yet been estimated.4:Taf989,<h2 data-number="1" id="sec:intro"><span class="header-section-number">1</span> Introduction</h2>
website/out/papers/coercive-power/index.txt:9:<p>The argument has four steps. Section <a class="xref" href="#sec:necessity">3</a> derives the coercive function from the axiom of defection (Ax5). A deterrence theorem shows that rule compliance above the rate set by agents’ temptations requires a nonzero sanction regime, and a second result shows that, when sanctioning is costly, sanctioners themselves need provisioning, a norm of punishment, a higher-order sanction or a direct stake in deterrence. Both results are stated at the level of the role, not of any institution, and the ethnographic record of stateless societies shows the minimal forms they predict. Section <a class="xref" href="#sec:comparative">5</a> compares the distribution of the function across six regime types with equal depth. Section <a class="xref" href="#sec:mechanisms">6</a> introduces the distinction that carries the paper’s argument about capture: the conduct margin of an enforcement apparatus, which measures how much it responds to what people do, and its allegiance margin, which measures how much it responds to whose side they are on. The two margins are separable, so a strong coercive function can coexist with zero capture. When capacity is limited, allegiance targeting weakens deterrence for at least one group; when opponents are targeted regardless of conduct, it also raises the volume of coercion against them. Section <a class="xref" href="#sec:measurement">7</a> turns these results into indicators and falsifiable hypotheses, and Section <a class="xref" href="#sec:revelation">8</a> reads Revelation 13 against Romans 13 as two typological images of the sword: one conditioned on conduct, the other on worship.</p>
website/out/papers/coercive-power/index.txt:17:<p class="thm-head"><span class="thm-label">Definition 2.1</span><span class="thm-name">Coercive act, sanction and sanction function</span></p><p>A <em>coercive act</em> is a cost imposed on an agent by one or more other agents in response to the agent’s conduct or status. The cost may be material (fines, seizure, detention, injury, death), relational (withdrawal of cooperation, exclusion from exchange, exile) or reputational (ridicule, gossip, loss of standing). A <em>sanction</em> is a coercive act that responds to an observed or alleged violation of a rule. The <em>sanction function</em> <span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi mathvariant="sans-serif">C</mi></mrow>\mathsf{C}</math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="katex-base"><span class="katex-strut" style="height:0.6944em;"></span><span class="mord mathsf">C</span></span></span></span> of a collective is the set of practices by which violations are detected and sanctions are decided and delivered. It is <em>implemented</em> if, when violations occur and are detected, they are met with sanctions with non-trivial regularity, whether through designated offices, through coalitions formed for the occasion, or through dispersed individual responses.</p>
website/out/papers/coercive-power/index.txt:19:<p>The definition is broad on the form of the cost and narrow on what makes a cost a sanction. Costs that fall on an agent regardless of what the agent does or is (a drought, a tax schedule applied equally to all) are not coercive acts. Costs that respond to status rather than to a rule violation, such as surveillance of an opposition party whose members have broken no rule, are coercive acts but not sanctions. The coercive layer records both, because the distinction between them is what Definition <a class="xref" href="#def:coercive-power:margins">2.5</a> measures.</p>

Concentration in either sense is distinct from Weber’s monopoly of legitimate violence, which Part&nbsp;II (Section&nbsp;2) uses to describe the relation between rule-making and enforcement. Weber’s monopoly concerns the claim that only authorized agents may use force. It is a statement about the dependency of coercion on legitimation, not about who commands. A polity can make that claim successfully while dispersing command across many agencies, and a polity can concentrate command while failing to make the claim credible.</p>

It includes <span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow>i</math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="katex-base"><span class="katex-strut" style="height:0.6595em;"></span><span class="mord mathnormal">i</span></span></span></span>’s own optimal future behavior, which may itself change after a violation; an agent excluded from cooperation, for example, faces different future margins from one in good standing. Under the payoff assumption of Section <a class="xref" href="#sec:necessity">3</a>, a violation affects <span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow>i</math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="katex-base"><span class="katex-strut" style="height:0.6595em;"></span><span class="mord mathnormal">i</span></span></span></span>’s future only through other agents’ responses, so the margin is zero whenever <span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>σ</mi><mrow><mo>−</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub></mrow>\sigma_{-i}</math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="katex-base"><span class="katex-strut" style="height:0.6389em;vertical-align:-0.2083em;"></span><span class="mord"><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right:0.0359em;">σ</span><span class="msupsub"><span class="vlist-t vlist-t2"><span class="vlist-r"><span class="vlist" style="height:0.3117em;"><span style="top:-2.55em;margin-left:-0.0359em;margin-right:0.05em;"><span class="pstrut" style="height:2.7em;"></span><span class="katex-sizing reset-size6 size3 mtight"><span class="mord mtight"><span class="mord mtight">−</span><span class="mord mathnormal mtight">i</span></span></span></span></span><span class="vlist-s">​</span></span><span class="vlist-r"><span class="vlist" style="height:0.2083em;"><span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span> does not condition on <span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow>i</math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="katex-base"><span class="katex-strut" style="height:0.6595em;"></span><span class="mord mathnormal">i</span></span></span></span>’s violations. A positive margin therefore requires that others respond to <span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow>i</math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="katex-base"><span class="katex-strut" style="height:0.6595em;"></span><span class="mord mathnormal">i</span></span></span></span>’s violation in a way that lowers <span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow>i</math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="katex-base"><span class="katex-strut" style="height:0.6595em;"></span><span class="mord mathnormal">i</span></span></span></span>’s payoff. The response may be a beating, a lawsuit, a boycott or a refusal to share meat. The definition does not ask who responds or whether they hold an office.</p>

website/out/papers/coercive-power/index.txt:51:<p>Proposition&nbsp;A for the coercive pillar asserts the implemented function of Definition <a class="xref" href="#def:coercive-power:sanction">2.1</a>: violations, when they occur and are detected, are met with sanctions with non-trivial regularity. It follows from Theorem <a class="xref" href="#thm:coercive-power:necessity">3.4</a> under the bridge assumption together with two further conditions, that members best-respond to their temptations and that <span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>G</mi></mrow>G</math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="katex-base"><span class="katex-strut" style="height:0.6833em;"></span><span class="mord mathnormal">G</span></span></span></span> has unbounded support, so that violations occur on the path of play and the threatened sanctions are actually delivered. The bridge carries the empirical content of the coercive pillar’s place in Proposition&nbsp;A. It is not true by definition: it would fail for a collective whose every rule is one that almost nobody is tempted to break, and Section <a class="xref" href="#sec:counter">3.5</a> states how to test it with a measurement of <span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow>p</math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="katex-base"><span class="katex-strut" style="height:0.625em;vertical-align:-0.1944em;"></span><span class="mord mathnormal">p</span></span></span></span> that is independent of sanction practices. The theorem is a necessity statement about a role, in the sense required by Part&nbsp;VII: some agents must respond to violations in a way that costs the violator. It is silent on who those agents are, on whether they specialize, and on whether the cost is physical. It also gives two quantitative floors. website/out/papers/coercive-power/index.txt:67:<p>A positive margin is a threat. Definition <a class="xref" href="#def:coercive-power:sanction">2.1</a> counts the function as implemented only if violations, when they occur, are actually met with sanctions. The two notions coincide whenever violations occur on the path of play. website/out/papers/coercive-power/index.txt:82:<p>The proposition is a disjunction, and its interpretation needs care. Term (a) is the dependency <span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi mathvariant="sans-serif">F</mi><mo>→</mo><mi mathvariant="sans-serif">C</mi></mrow>\mathsf{F}\to \mathsf{C}</math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="katex-base"><span class="katex-strut" style="height:0.6944em;"></span><span class="mord mathsf">F</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right:0.2778em;"></span><span class="mrel">→</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right:0.2778em;"></span></span><span class="katex-base"><span class="katex-strut" style="height:0.6944em;"></span><span class="mord mathsf">C</span></span></span></span>: paid soldiers and police are provisioned out of resources that someone allocates. Term (b) is the dependency <span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi mathvariant="sans-serif">I</mi><mo>→</mo><mi mathvariant="sans-serif">C</mi></mrow>\mathsf{I}\to \mathsf{C}</math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="katex-base"><span class="katex-strut" style="height:0.6944em;"></span><span class="mord mathsf">I</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right:0.2778em;"></span><span class="mrel">→</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right:0.2778em;"></span></span><span class="katex-base"><span class="katex-strut" style="height:0.6944em;"></span><span class="mord mathsf">C</span></span></span></span>: a norm that makes punishing violators honorable, or a belief that the sanctioning authority is legitimate, supplies the reward. Term (c) is coercion applied to the coercers. In repeated games it can close the regress in equilibrium without transfers or intrinsic rewards: community-enforcement equilibria, in which those who fail to punish are themselves punished, need only that agents coordinate on the same punishment norm. Whether that coordination counts as legitimation is a question for Part&nbsp;IV, and this paper does not settle it by definition. Term (d) does not route the dependency through <span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi mathvariant="sans-serif">F</mi></mrow>\mathsf{F}</math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="katex-base"><span class="katex-strut" style="height:0.6944em;"></span><span class="mord mathsf">F</span></span></span></span> or <span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi mathvariant="sans-serif">I</mi></mrow>\mathsf{I}</math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="katex-base"><span class="katex-strut" style="height:0.6944em;"></span><span class="mord mathsf">I</span></span></span></span>. The structure parallels Proposition&nbsp;3.6 of Part&nbsp;III, where an effective judicial determination needs legitimacy or sanction: in both cases the incoming dependency is a disjunction, which Part&nbsp;VII must treat as a hyperedge of the dependency digraph rather than as separate arcs.</p>

website/out/papers/coercive-power/index.txt:100:<p>Both bounds fall as <span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>r</mi></mrow>r</math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="katex-base"><span class="katex-strut" style="height:0.4306em;"></span><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right:0.0278em;">r</span></span></span></span> rises: an agent at the start of a long exclusion has less to lose from a further violation, which is why such profiles are usually combined with graduated sanctions or with longer exclusion for repeat violators. The proposition computes margins; it does not show that the profile is an equilibrium for the excluders. Each excluder forgoes its own surplus from cooperating with the violator, which is the second-order cost of Proposition <a class="xref" href="#prop:coercive-power:second-order">3.6</a>. Extending the profile so that anyone who cooperates with an excluded agent is also excluded supplies term (c). Whether the extended profile is an equilibrium depends on whether the surplus an agent would lose by being excluded from the whole group exceeds the surplus it forgoes by withholding cooperation from one violator, and we do not claim that it is an equilibrium in general. The ethnographic record suggests that terms (b) and (d) also operate: people are angered by violations, and in small groups each person’s response matters.</p>
website/out/papers/coercive-power/index.txt:147:<p>The strongest attempt to refute the necessity of coercion appeals to self-enforcing cooperation. Axelrod showed that reciprocal strategies can sustain cooperation without a central authority (Axelrod 1984). Greif showed that the eleventh-century Maghribi traders enforced agency contracts through a coalition in which cheated merchants were refused future employment by all members (Greif 1993). Edwards and Ogilvie dispute this reading and argue that the traders also relied on formal legal institutions (Edwards and Ogilvie 2012); on either reading the case contains sanctions. Ellickson found that cattle ranchers in Shasta County settled disputes by neighborly norms rather than by law (Ellickson 1991). None of these is a counterexample. In each case an agent’s continuation payoff depends on the agent’s own past conduct: the reciprocator retaliates, the coalition refuses to deal, and the neighbor gossips or engages in self-help. Each mechanism is a sanction regime in the sense of Definition <a class="xref" href="#def:coercive-power:regime">2.4</a>. What these cases refute is the Hobbesian inference from the need for sanctions to the need for a sovereign.</p>
website/out/papers/coercive-power/index.txt:159:<p>If coercion is provisioned (term (a) of Proposition <a class="xref" href="#prop:coercive-power:second-order">3.6</a>), the agents who hold it can turn it against those who provision them. Civil-military relations theory is the study of this problem. Huntington proposed objective civilian control: a professional officer corps, autonomous in military matters and politically neutral (Huntington 1957). Janowitz replied that professionalism alone does not secure neutrality and that the military should be integrated into civilian society as a constabulary force (Janowitz 1960). Finer catalogued the forms of military intervention in politics (Finer 1962), and Huntington and Perlmutter described praetorian societies in which armed forces become ordinary political contestants (Huntington 1968; Perlmutter 1969). Feaver recast the relationship as a principal-agent problem in which civilians choose monitoring mechanisms and soldiers choose whether to work or shirk (Feaver 1999; Feaver 2003). Kohn emphasized that civilian control is a practice that must be exercised, not merely a constitutional provision (Kohn 1997).</p>
website/out/papers/coercive-power/index.txt:160:<p>Authoritarian rulers face the guardian problem in a sharper form. Svolik showed that dictators face two separate problems: sharing power with the allied elites who help them rule, and controlling the masses they rule (Svolik 2012). Coercive agents are useful against the second problem and dangerous in the first. Quinlivan described the coup-proofing practices of Middle Eastern regimes: reliance on family, ethnic and religious loyalties, the creation of parallel military forces, and multiple overlapping internal security agencies (Quinlivan 1999). Pilster and Böhmelt found that coup-proofing reduced battlefield effectiveness in interstate wars between 1967 and 1999 (Pilster and Böhmelt 2011). Greitens argued that the design of coercive institutions depends on whether rulers perceive their main threat as coming from elites or from the masses: elite threats favor fragmented and socially exclusive organizations, mass threats favor unified and inclusive ones, and these designs in turn shape patterns of state violence (Greitens 2016). Slater showed that elites who fear contentious mass politics may accept stronger coercive and extractive institutions as protection pacts (Slater 2010).</p>
website/out/papers/coercive-power/index.txt:163:<p>Whether coercive agents carry out repression is not guaranteed. Bellin attributed the durability of Middle Eastern authoritarianism to the will and capacity of coercive apparatuses to repress, and after the Arab uprisings of 2011 she examined why some militaries defected and others did not (Bellin 2004; Bellin 2012). Albrecht and Ohl applied Hirschman’s categories of exit, voice and loyalty to military behavior during unrest (Albrecht and Ohl 2016), and Chenoweth and Stephan argued that nonviolent campaigns succeed in part by inducing defections among security forces (Chenoweth and Stephan 2011). Gerschewski placed repression beside legitimation and co-optation as the three pillars of autocratic stability (Gerschewski 2013).</p>
website/out/papers/coercive-power/index.txt:173:<p>Concentration differs sharply between the military and the police. Command of the armed forces is concentrated in a national executive, so the military contributes a large share to <span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mi>H</mi><mi mathvariant="sans-serif">C</mi></msup></mrow>H^{\mathsf{C}}</math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="katex-base"><span class="katex-strut" style="height:0.8491em;"></span><span class="mord"><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right:0.0813em;">H</span><span class="msupsub"><span class="vlist-t"><span class="vlist-r"><span class="vlist" style="height:0.8491em;"><span style="top:-3.063em;margin-right:0.05em;"><span class="pstrut" style="height:2.7em;"></span><span class="katex-sizing reset-size6 size3 mtight"><span class="mord mtight"><span class="mord mathsf mtight">C</span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span>, while legislative control of budgets divides authority over provisioning. Policing in the United States is dispersed across federal, state and local agencies, each answering to a different elected authority, which lowers <span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mi>H</mi><mi mathvariant="sans-serif">C</mi></msup></mrow>H^{\mathsf{C}}</math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="katex-base"><span class="katex-strut" style="height:0.8491em;"></span><span class="mord"><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right:0.0813em;">H</span><span class="msupsub"><span class="vlist-t"><span class="vlist-r"><span class="vlist" style="height:0.8491em;"><span style="top:-3.063em;margin-right:0.05em;"><span class="pstrut" style="height:2.7em;"></span><span class="katex-sizing reset-size6 size3 mtight"><span class="mord mtight"><span class="mord mathsf mtight">C</span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span> for ordinary enforcement. The theory of civilian control was developed largely on the American case: Huntington’s objective control, Janowitz’s constabulary force and Feaver’s agency model all address how elected civilians can command a professional military that they cannot fully monitor (Huntington 1957; Janowitz 1960; Feaver 2003). Accountability rests on component (1) of <span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mi>Q</mi><mi mathvariant="sans-serif">C</mi></msup></mrow>Q^{\mathsf{C}}</math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="katex-base"><span class="katex-strut" style="height:1.0435em;vertical-align:-0.1944em;"></span><span class="mord"><span class="mord mathnormal">Q</span><span class="msupsub"><span class="vlist-t"><span class="vlist-r"><span class="vlist" style="height:0.8491em;"><span style="top:-3.063em;margin-right:0.05em;"><span class="pstrut" style="height:2.7em;"></span><span class="katex-sizing reset-size6 size3 mtight"><span class="mord mtight"><span class="mord mathsf mtight">C</span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span>, appointment and removal by elected civilians; on components (2) and (4), judicial authorization of searches and the civil and criminal liability of agents; and on component (6), legislative scrutiny of budgets. Kohn argued that these provisions secure control only when civilians actually exercise them (Kohn 1997).</p>
website/out/papers/coercive-power/index.txt:174:<p>The capture hypothesis specific to this regime type is that concentrated private interests shape the use of coercion. It meets the source paper’s standard for a capture link only if three things are shown: privileged access by a private party, a weakening of the accountability that would otherwise apply, and material evidence that the access changed an enforcement outcome (Largo 2026). Eisenhower’s warning is evidence that a senior insider regarded the risk as serious; it is not evidence that capture occurred in any particular decision. A better documented episode comes from industrial conflict. The federal Commission on Industrial Relations reported in 1915 that “practically every industrial State has at some relatively recent time permitted its institutions to be used by one party or the other to an industrial dispute (almost without exception the employers)”. It found that sheriffs in many counties deputized guards “in the employment and pay of corporations” and that militia were at times recruited from corporate guards and employees (Commission on Industrial Relations 1915, pp.&nbsp;147 to 148). Each element of the capture link is present in that finding: privileged access through deputization, the displacement of publicly accountable police by employer-paid agents, and enforcement outcomes against strikers. In the notation of Definition <a class="xref" href="#def:coercive-power:margins">2.5</a>, the allegiance margin was indexed by the side a person took in an industrial dispute. The report was itself the check. A public commission with investigative powers documented the practice and recommended rules for the conduct of the militia (Commission on Industrial Relations 1915).</p>
website/out/papers/coercive-power/index.txt:199:<p>Bourbon France built one of the largest armies in Europe. Lynn traced its growth between 1610 and 1715 (Lynn 1997). Rowlands showed that under Louis XIV royal service and private interest were intertwined: officers invested their own resources in their units, and the crown relied on that investment while trying to control it (Rowlands 2002). Venal commissions integrate finance and force at the level of the individual officer, who is both a creditor of the state and an agent of its force. Parker’s thesis of a military revolution, in which new fortifications and tactics drove the growth of armies and states, frames these developments (Parker 1988), and Tilly’s account of coercion and capital explains why monarchies with access to commercial credit could field such armies (Tilly 1990).</p>
website/out/papers/coercive-power/index.txt:208:<p>Concentration in secular democracies varies with constitutional structure. Integration with the political pillar is limited because civilian appointment is shared among elected bodies and constrained by professional norms of neutrality. The dependency on the judicial pillar runs through warrants and liability, and the dependency on legitimation runs through public acceptance of the constitution and of the police, which Tyler’s research measures directly (Tyler 1990). The main risk specific to this type is that oversight bodies depend on information that the overseen agencies control, which is the principal-agent problem of Feaver’s model applied to intelligence (Feaver 2003). The episodes of this subsection and of Section <a class="xref" href="#sec:socdem">5.3</a> show that risk realized for decades before legislatures intervened.</p>

website/out/papers/coercive-power/index.txt:315:<p>The source paper’s second proposition holds that effective independent review and voice reduce the probability that attempted capture yields persistent unreviewable outcomes (Largo 2026). In the coercive pillar the checks act on the margins directly. Judicial authorization of intrusive measures raises the evidentiary threshold for coercive acts, which lowers <span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>ψ</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo separator="true">,</mo><mi>y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow>\psi(0,y)</math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="katex-base"><span class="katex-strut" style="height:1em;vertical-align:-0.25em;"></span><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right:0.0359em;">ψ</span><span class="mopen">(</span><span class="mord">0</span><span class="mpunct">,</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right:0.1667em;"></span><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right:0.0359em;">y</span><span class="mclose">)</span></span></span></span> for everyone and so raises the conduct margin. Independent complaint bodies make a positive allegiance margin visible and therefore costly. Individual liability of agents for unlawful force raises the private cost of arbitrary coercion for the coercers themselves. Protected refusal of unlawful orders introduces a veto at the point of execution: when soldiers or police refuse to fire on peaceful crowds, the allegiance margin is cut off at its source, which is the mechanism that Chenoweth and Stephan and Albrecht and Ohl identify in security-force defection (Chenoweth and Stephan 2011; Albrecht and Ohl 2016).</p>
website/out/papers/coercive-power/index.txt:570:a:T641,Every governance system must decide who enforces its rules. This paper derives the coercive function from one axiom, that members sometimes have reason to break rules, and compares how six regime types distribute it. A deterrence theorem shows that when the share of agents tempted to violate a rule exceeds the violation rate the collective can tolerate, compliance requires that violators’ continuation payoffs fall because of their own conduct. A sanction regime of some kind is therefore necessary, but no particular institution is. Gossip, ostracism and coalition action against would-be dominants meet this requirement as well as police do, as the ethnography of the Nuer, the Ju/’hoansi, Amazonian societies and Ostrom’s commons documents. A second result shows why, where sanctions are costly public goods and higher-order sanctions are absent, coercion at scale depends on provisioning or on shared norms of punishment. The paper then separates two properties of any enforcement apparatus: its conduct margin, how much more likely a violator is to be sanctioned than a complier, and its allegiance margin, how much more likely an opponent is to be sanctioned than a supporter. The two margins vary independently, so the necessity of coercion does not imply its capture. When capacity is limited, allegiance targeting weakens deterrence for at least one group; when opponents are targeted regardless of conduct, it also raises the volume of coercion against them, so spending and arrest counts mismeasure coercive power. The main limitation is that neither margin has yet been estimated.b:T641,Every governance system must decide who enforces its rules. This paper derives the coercive function from one axiom, that members sometimes have reason to break rules, and compares how six regime types distribute it. A deterrence theorem shows that when the share of agents tempted to violate a rule exceeds the violation rate the collective can tolerate, compliance requires that violators’ continuation payoffs fall because of their own conduct. A sanction regime of some kind is therefore necessary, but no particular institution is. Gossip, ostracism and coalition action against would-be dominants meet this requirement as well as police do, as the ethnography of the Nuer, the Ju/’hoansi, Amazonian societies and Ostrom’s commons documents. A second result shows why, where sanctions are costly public goods and higher-order sanctions are absent, coercion at scale depends on provisioning or on shared norms of punishment. The paper then separates two properties of any enforcement apparatus: its conduct margin, how much more likely a violator is to be sanctioned than a complier, and its allegiance margin, how much more likely an opponent is to be sanctioned than a supporter. The two margins vary independently, so the necessity of coercion does not imply its capture. When capacity is limited, allegiance targeting weakens deterrence for at least one group; when opponents are targeted regardless of conduct, it also raises the volume of coercion against them, so spending and arrest counts mismeasure coercive power. website/out/papers/productive-power/index.txt:114:<p class="thm-head"><span class="thm-label">Assumption 3.2</span><span class="thm-name">No manna</span></p><p>Inflows are produced: <span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>Y</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>&gt;</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow>Y_t&gt;0</math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="katex-base"><span class="katex-strut" style="height:0.8333em;vertical-align:-0.15em;"></span><span class="mord"><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right:0.2222em;">Y</span><span class="msupsub"><span class="vlist-t vlist-t2"><span class="vlist-r"><span class="vlist" style="height:0.2806em;"><span style="top:-2.55em;margin-left:-0.2222em;margin-right:0.05em;"><span class="pstrut" style="height:2.7em;"></span><span class="katex-sizing reset-size6 size3 mtight"><span class="mord mathnormal mtight">t</span></span></span></span><span class="vlist-s">​</span></span><span class="vlist-r"><span class="vlist" style="height:0.15em;"><span></span></span></span></span></span></span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right:0.2778em;"></span><span class="mrel">&gt;</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right:0.2778em;"></span></span><span class="katex-base"><span class="katex-strut" style="height:0.6444em;"></span><span class="mord">0</span></span></span></span> only if some agent, inside or outside the collective, performs productive activity in period <span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow>t</math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="katex-base"><span class="katex-strut" style="height:0.6151em;"></span><span class="mord mathnormal">t</span></span></span></span> or owns, operates or maintains equipment that does.</p>
website/out/papers/ideological-power/index.txt:9:<p>The ideological pillar poses these tasks in a sharp form. Its institutions include universities, churches, mosques and seminaries, newsrooms, schools, academies of science and medical bodies. These institutions command trust because they are expected to report what they find rather than what rulers prefer. They can check capture by disclosing errors and refusing endorsement. They can also enable capture by lending credibility to rules that serve a narrow coalition. Nothing in this paper implies that expertise, medicine, science or any faith is fraudulent. The source framework says plainly that a hospital is not a propaganda organ and a professor is not an agent of command (Largo 2026). The analytical question is when the independence that gives these authorities their value is preserved, and when it is lost.</p>
website/out/papers/ideological-power/index.txt:492:<p>The second beast performs the function this paper studies. It produces belief in the authority of the first beast, and it does so through public signs performed “in the sight of men” (13:13), which are public events in the sense of Definition&nbsp;<a class="xref" href="#def:ideological-power:public-signal">2.4</a>. The contextual reading identifies it with the agents of the imperial cult in Asia. Price (1984) showed that the cult in Asia Minor was organized largely by the cities and their elites, who used it to represent imperial power within their own civic religion, and Friesen (2001) examined its provincial institutions. The legitimation of Roman rule was thus supplied locally, by elites who gained standing from it. In the vocabulary of Section&nbsp;<a class="xref" href="#sec:mechanisms">6</a>, it rested on privileged access exchanged for endorsement.</p>
website/out/papers/ideological-power/index.txt:505:<p>A defender of science, medicine or religion may object that classing these institutions as ideological power disparages them. The classification concerns the function they perform for coordination, not the truth of what they teach. A physician who certifies that a vaccine is safe, a jurist who explains a rule of inheritance and a priest who instructs a congregation each change beliefs that others rely on. The results of this paper give independent authorities their value: their endorsement is informative because it is independent, and they protect the public precisely when a coalition’s rule is unsound. The source framework’s caution applies throughout: a hospital is not a propaganda organ and a professor is not an agent of command (Largo 2026). The paper is silent on the truth of any faith’s claims, and the theological reading of Section&nbsp;<a class="xref" href="#sec:revelation">8</a> rests on a distinction that Revelation itself draws between witness and enforced display.</p>

website/out/papers/formalized-state/index.txt:82:<p>The refined axioms are empirical claims about human collectives, not logical truths. Each can be false of some conceivable collective. The arc out of coercion that the theorem uses, <span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi mathvariant="sans-serif">C</mi><mo>→</mo><mi mathvariant="sans-serif">F</mi></mrow>\mathsf{C}\to\mathsf{F}</math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="katex-base"><span class="katex-strut" style="height:0.6944em;"></span><span class="mord mathsf">C</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right:0.2778em;"></span><span class="mrel">→</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right:0.2778em;"></span></span><span class="katex-base"><span class="katex-strut" style="height:0.6944em;"></span><span class="mord mathsf">F</span></span></span></span>, rests on X5 and on Lemma 3.3 of <a class="xpart" href="/papers/coercive-power/#lem:coercive-power:deterrence">Part V</a>, which say only that without any response to breach the breach rate exceeds tolerance. Bilateral exclusion is one such response. When it is the only one, coercion is exercised in its most dispersed form, and the arc is unaffected.</p>

The contested plot is the field the members cultivate, so production uses an input under an anticipable assignment (X1). The environment alternates between two states, and each change brings a new kind of claim that the old rotation rule does not cover, which the members settle by voting a new rule (X2). The residual disputes concern the application of the rotation rule to boundary cases (X3). Members are tempted to take the field out of turn with <span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>&gt;</mo><mi>θ</mi></mrow>p&gt;\theta</math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="katex-base"><span class="katex-strut" style="height:0.7335em;vertical-align:-0.1944em;"></span><span class="mord mathnormal">p</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right:0.2778em;"></span><span class="mrel">&gt;</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right:0.2778em;"></span></span><span class="katex-base"><span class="katex-strut" style="height:0.6944em;"></span><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right:0.0278em;">θ</span></span></span></span>, and a member who does so pays a fine and is made to return the field, so the conflict counts as settled (X5). website/out/papers/financial-power/index.html:156:<p>The economic theory of regulation asks how resource holders shape the rules that govern them. Stigler’s theory of economic regulation treats regulation as a good demanded by industries and supplied by the state, so that regulatory agencies tend to serve the regulated (Stigler 1971). Peltzman generalized the model: a regulator balances producer and consumer pressure, so outcomes fall between pure capture and pure public interest (Peltzman 1976). Becker showed that competition among pressure groups limits the transfers any one group can extract, because deadweight losses grow with the size of the transfer and mobilize the losers (Becker 1983). Laffont and Tirole recast capture as a principal-supervisor-agent problem in which the danger of collusion between the supervisor and the regulated firm shapes the optimal design of incentives (Laffont and Tirole 1991). Grossman and Helpman modeled trade protection as the outcome of contribution schedules offered to an incumbent government (Grossman and Helpman 1994). Dal Bó surveys the theory and evidence (Dal Bó 2006), and Carpenter and Moss insist on a demanding definition: capture requires showing that regulation was directed away from the public interest and toward the regulated industry by the industry’s own intent and action, not merely that the industry benefited (Carpenter and Moss 2014). That standard is the same one the capture link of Largo (2026) encodes.</p>
website/out/papers/financial-power/index.html:173:<p>Formal concentration overstates effective concentration. Gregory’s study of the Soviet archives shows that the top leadership could not allocate everything and bargained constantly with ministries and enterprises that held better information about their own capacities (Gregory 2004). Berliner’s interviews with former Soviet managers documented the informal procurement agents who obtained scarce inputs outside the plan, and the networks of favors through which managers met targets (Berliner 1957); Ledeneva reconstructed the economy of favors, known as blat, that ran alongside the formal allocation of goods in the late Soviet period (Ledeneva 1998). These informal channels lowered effective concentration while also lowering contestability, since favors were by nature unrecorded and unreviewable. Kornai’s soft budget constraint completes the picture: enterprises expected rescue from their administrative superiors, so loss did not lead to exit, and the allocation of credit followed bargaining power rather than performance (Kornai 1986).</p>

This paper treats that settlement as the financial pillar of a six-function model of governance and asks who controls resources across regime types. From a scarcity axiom and an explicit assumption that unsettled conflicts carry a positive hazard of dissolution, we prove that a collective with no recognized allocation regularity cannot persist with probability bounded away from zero, and that in any collective that does persist the share of conflicts settled by such a regularity tends to one. The result concerns a function, not an institution: in foraging bands the regularity is a sharing norm, and control is dispersed close to the minimum concentration the index allows. We then prove that the necessity of the pillar places no restriction on its concentration or contestability, show that aggregating subdomains understates concentration by exactly the cross-domain variance of control shares, and derive conditional comparative statics under which resource holders convert wealth into influence over rules. A comparison of market-capitalist societies, communist party-states, social democracies, Islamic states, Catholic monarchies and secular democracies finds the same function held by different institutions, with documented capture episodes and documented checks in every type. Seven hypotheses with stated falsifiers make the capture claim testable. Revelation 13 and 18 are read typologically as images of economic participation conditioned on allegiance. The main limitation is that no coded cross-regime dataset yet exists, so the comparative claims remain qualitative.a:T88fdc,"])</script><script>self.__next_f.push([1,"\u003ch2 data-number=\"1\" id=\"sec:intro\"\u003e\u003cspan class=\"header-section-number\"\u003e1\u003c/span\u003e Introduction\u003c/h2\u003e\n\u003cp\u003eEvery polity decides who controls its resources, whether or not it has a treasury, a bank, or a word for property. A foraging camp decides who carves the meat and who receives which portion. A pastoral lineage decides whose cattle pay a bridewealth or a blood debt. A medieval caliphate assigns revenues to a treasury and endowments to trustees, an early modern monarchy pledges future taxes to its bankers, a Soviet ministry allocates steel by plan, and a modern democracy delegates the supply of money to an independent central bank. The institutions differ almost completely. The problem they solve does not.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp\u003eThis paper is the first of seven Parts of a series whose thesis is that the ideology of governance changes while its institutional functions remain. The series follows the framework of Largo (2026), which models a polity as a directed multiplex network whose layers record distinct mechanisms of constraint, and which asks when concentration and coordination across those layers turn into unaccountable domination. The series uses six pillars: financial power\u0026nbsp;\u003cspan class=\"katex\"\u003e\u003cspan class=\"katex-mathml\"\u003e\u003cmath style=\"margin-right:0.0139em;\"\u003eW\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/span\u003e (who produces the wealth that sustains everything). \u003ca class=\"xpart\" href=\"/papers/formalized-state/\"\u003ePart VII\u003c/a\u003e (\u003ca href=\"/papers/formalized-state/\"\u003eLong 2026b\u003c/a\u003e) proves the general claim, called Proposition\u0026nbsp;A, that every functioning governance system contains all six functions and the dependencies among them, and it proves that this structural necessity does not imply Proposition\u0026nbsp;B, the contingent and measurable claim that the functions have been captured by a coalition that escapes independent accountability.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp\u003eThe financial pillar is the one most easily misread. Popular usage equates control of resources with capitalists, bankers, or a single class, and so treats the existence of the pillar as an accusation. The argument here runs the other way. Resource command exists in a hunter-gatherer camp, where it is held by everyone at once through sharing norms; what varies across polities is how concentrated it is, how contestable it is, and how tightly it is coupled to rule-making, adjudication, belief, coercion, and work. A theory that cannot separate the existence of the function from its concentration will find domination everywhere and therefore explain nothing.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp\u003eThe necessity of the function and the contingency of its concentration can both be proved. From the scarcity axiom of the series and an explicit assumption that unsettled conflict risks dissolution, a collective with no recognized way of settling claims loses its chance of survival geometrically over time, and in a collective that survives almost every conflict is settled by such a procedure (Proposition \u003ca class=\"xref\" href=\"#prop:financial-power:necessity\"\u003e3.3\u003c/a\u003e). The same necessity places no restriction on how concentrated or contestable control is (Proposition \u003ca class=\"xref\" href=\"#prop:financial-power:nonimplication\"\u003e3.5\u003c/a\u003e); this is the pillar-level case of the non-implication that \u003ca class=\"xpart\" href=\"/papers/formalized-state/\"\u003ePart VII\u003c/a\u003e proves for all six pillars.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp\u003eThree further results make the comparison measurable. Aggregate concentration understates the concentration of subdomains such as credit, land, and the public budget by exactly the cross-domain variance of control shares (Proposition \u003ca class=\"xref\" href=\"#prop:financial-power:aggregation-gap\"\u003e2.5\u003c/a\u003e). A resource holder’s investment in influence over other pillars rises with its share and falls with the contestability of the receiving pillar (Proposition \u003ca class=\"xref\" href=\"#prop:financial-power:influence\"\u003e6.2\u003c/a\u003e). And lenders to a sovereign are protected by the threat of exclusion from future credit, not by control of legislation, whenever the ruler’s future need for credit is large enough (Proposition \u003ca class=\"xref\" href=\"#prop:financial-power:sovereign-credit\"\u003e6.4\u003c/a\u003e). The six regime types of the series are then compared with the same questions and the same standard of evidence, and seven hypotheses are stated together with the observations that would falsify them.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cp\u003eTwo scope commitments govern everything that follows. The phrase “Beast System” names the universal six-function structure that \u003ca class=\"xpart\" href=\"/papers/formalized-state/\"\u003ePart VII\u003c/a\u003e proves present in every governance system; it is never a label for a religion, a people, a profession, a regime, or a person. And the comparison asks how the universal function is distributed in each regime type, not whether a civilization “has” it. Because every type has it, the comparison is even-handed by construction, and the evidentiary burden falls entirely on claims of capture.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003ch2 data-number=\"2\" id=\"sec:pillar\"\u003e\u003cspan class=\"header-section-number\"\u003e2\u003c/span\u003e The financial pillar in the multiplex network\u003c/h2\u003e\n\u003ch3 data-number=\"2.1\" id=\"shared-notation\"\u003e\u003cspan class=\"header-section-number\"\u003e2.1\u003c/span\u003e Shared notation\u003c/h3\u003e\n\u003cp\u003eThe series inherits its formal objects from Largo (2026) and does not redefine them. prevails, together with the related decisions of who may use a good, who may store it, and what is held in reserve.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003c/div\u003e\n\u003cp\u003eScarcity in this sense is relative to claims, not absolute. A group can be materially comfortable and still face conflicts, because the meat of one animal, the best grazing in a dry season, or the revenue of one year is claimed by more people, or for more purposes, than it can satisfy. This is the scarcity axiom of the series (Ax1: resources are finite and claims on them conflict), whose general statement and refinement belong to \u003ca class=\"xpart\" href=\"/papers/formalized-state/\"\u003ePart VII\u003c/a\u003e.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cdiv id=\"def:financial-power:settlement\" class=\"definition thm thm-definition\"\u003e\n\u003cp class=\"thm-head\"\u003e\u003cspan class=\"thm-label\"\u003eDefinition 2.2\u003c/span\u003e\u003cspan class=\"thm-name\"\u003eSettlement\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eA conflict is \u003cem\u003esettled\u003c/em\u003e when it is resolved by a procedure that belongs to the collective’s repertoire, meaning that (a) the procedure applies to a class of situations rather than to a single instance, (b) members can anticipate the resulting assignment from a description of the procedure and of the situation, and (c) members comply with the assignment or are held to it by others. A conflict resolved without such a procedure, by unregulated contest whose outcome depends on whoever prevails in the moment, is \u003cem\u003eunsettled\u003c/em\u003e. The \u003cem\u003efinancial pillar\u003c/em\u003e of a collective is the set of procedures that settle its conflicts, together with the actors who operate them.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003c/div\u003e\n\u003cp\u003eThe definition is deliberately broad on the side of form and narrow on the side of function. A sharing norm, an ownership rule with voluntary exchange, a plan target, a waqf deed, a credit contract, a lottery, and a ritualized contest with known rules all settle conflicts. A brawl over a carcass does not, unless brawls themselves follow rules that the parties recognize. The broad side guards against the error of identifying the function with one institution; the narrow side keeps the definition from being satisfied by anything whatever.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cdiv id=\"def:financial-power:settlement-modes\" class=\"definition thm thm-definition\"\u003e\n\u003cp class=\"thm-head\"\u003e\u003cspan class=\"thm-label\"\u003eDefinition 2.3\u003c/span\u003e\u003cspan class=\"thm-name\"\u003eSettlement modes\u003c/span\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\u003cp\u003eA settlement procedure is classified by the source of the assignment it produces: a \u003cem\u003esharing norm\u003c/em\u003e assigns goods by a rule of distribution binding on the holder; \u003cem\u003eproperty and exchange\u003c/em\u003e assigns goods by prior entitlement and voluntary transfer at agreed terms; \u003cem\u003ecommand allocation\u003c/em\u003e assigns goods by the decision of an office; an \u003cem\u003eendowment\u003c/em\u003e assigns the yield of a dedicated asset to stated purposes under a trustee; \u003cem\u003ecredit\u003c/em\u003e assigns present goods against a promise of future repayment. Real procedures combine modes.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003c/div\u003e\n\u003cp\u003eThe modes are a coding device, not a typology of societies. A Ju/’hoansi camp uses sharing norms and also recognizes ownership of arrows; a market economy uses property and exchange and also command allocation through public budgets; an Ottoman province combined command allocation, endowments, and tax farms that were a form of credit to the treasury.\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003cdiv id=\"def:financial-power:allocation-regime\" class=\"definition thm thm-definition\"\u003e\n\u003cp class=\"thm-head\"\u003e\u003cspan class=\"thm-label\"\u003eDefinition 2.4\u003c/span\u003e\u003cspan class=\"thm-name\"\u003eAllocation The term is small when control is dispersed or when concentrated control is open to effective challenge, and it approaches one only when one actor holds the resources and nobody can contest how they are used.\u003cp\u003e\u003c/p\u003e\n\u003ch3 data-number=\"2.4\" id=\"subdomains-and-the-aggregation-gap\"\u003e\u003cspan class=\"header-section-number\"\u003e2.4\u003c/span\u003e Subdomains and the aggregation gap\u003c/h3\u003e\n\u003cp\u003eFinancial control is not one thing. A polity’s credit market, its land, its public budget, and its procurement system may each be held by different actors. website/out/papers/ideological-power/index.html:3:<p>The series rests on a single claim: the ideology changes; the institutional functions remain. Six questions recur in every governance system. Who controls the resources (<span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi mathvariant="sans-serif">F</mi></mrow>\mathsf{F}</math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="katex-base"><span class="katex-strut" style="height:0.6944em;"></span><span class="mord mathsf">F</span></span></span></span>)? Who makes the laws (<span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi mathvariant="sans-serif">P</mi></mrow>\mathsf{P}</math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="katex-base"><span class="katex-strut" style="height:0.6944em;"></span><span class="mord mathsf">P</span></span></span></span>)? Who interprets them (<span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi mathvariant="sans-serif">J</mi></mrow>\mathsf{J}</math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="katex-base"><span class="katex-strut" style="height:0.6944em;"></span><span class="mord mathsf">J</span></span></span></span>)? Who shapes the beliefs (<span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi mathvariant="sans-serif">I</mi></mrow>\mathsf{I}</math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="katex-base"><span class="katex-strut" style="height:0.6944em;"></span><span class="mord mathsf">I</span></span></span></span>)? Who enforces the rules (<span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi mathvariant="sans-serif">C</mi></mrow>\mathsf{C}</math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="katex-base"><span class="katex-strut" style="height:0.6944em;"></span><span class="mord mathsf">C</span></span></span></span>)? Who produces the wealth that sustains everything (<span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi mathvariant="sans-serif">W</mi></mrow>\mathsf{W}</math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="katex-base"><span class="katex-strut" style="height:0.6944em;"></span><span class="mord mathsf" style="margin-right:0.0139em;">W</span></span></span></span>)? The framework adapts the five-function Hierarchy of the Beast System developed by Largo (2026), whose rule function is split here into rule-making and adjudication. The name comes from Revelation 13, which describes a system binding authority, allegiance and economic participation. In this series the name designates the universal six-function structure itself. It is never a label for any religion, people, profession, regime or person.</p>
website/out/papers/ideological-power/index.html:4:<p>Proposition A of the series states that every functioning governance system contains the six functions together with dependency relations among them; <a class="xpart" href="/papers/formalized-state/">Part VII</a> proves it from axioms about collective life. Proposition B states that the functions become concentrated or coordinated so that independent accountability fails: unaccountable concentration <span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math Proposition A does not imply Proposition B, and <a class="xpart" href="/papers/formalized-state/">Part VII</a> proves the non-implication. The distinction matters for every pillar. The existence of a pillar is a structural fact; its capture is a contingent condition that must be measured.</p>
