website/out/papers/ideological-power/index.html:16:<p>Let <span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>R</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow>R_t</math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="katex-base"><span class="katex-strut" style="height:0.8333em;vertical-align:-0.15em;"></span><span class="mord"><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right:0.0077em;">R</span><span class="msupsub"><span class="vlist-t vlist-t2"><span class="vlist-r"><span class="vlist" style="height:0.2806em;"><span style="top:-2.55em;margin-left:-0.0077em;margin-right:0.05em;"><span class="pstrut" style="height:2.7em;"></span><span class="katex-sizing reset-size6 size3 mtight"><span class="mord mathnormal mtight">t</span></span></span></span><span class="vlist-s">​</span></span><span class="vlist-r"><span class="vlist" style="height:0.15em;"><span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span> denote the rule system in force in a collective at time <span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow>t</math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="katex-base"><span class="katex-strut" style="height:0.6151em;"></span><span class="mord mathnormal">t</span></span></span></span>, in the sense of Definition 2.1 of <a class="xpart" href="/papers/political-power/#def:political-power:rule-system">Part II</a>: the general prescriptions that members are expected to follow and that officials, where they exist, apply. The rule system includes rules that designate who holds office and rules that specify sanctions.</p>

A practice belongs to the class if it regularly changes members’ beliefs about these matters and if members rely on the changed beliefs when deciding whether to comply or cooperate.</p>
website/out/papers/ideological-power/index.html:22:<p class="thm-head"><span class="thm-label">Definition 2.2</span><span class="thm-name">Recognition and normative legitimacy</span></p><p>A belief system supports <em>recognition</em> of <span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>R</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow>R_t</math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="katex-base"><span class="katex-strut" style="height:0.8333em;vertical-align:-0.15em;"></span><span class="mord"><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right:0.0077em;">R</span><span class="msupsub"><span class="vlist-t vlist-t2"><span class="vlist-r"><span class="vlist" style="height:0.2806em;"><span style="top:-2.55em;margin-left:-0.0077em;margin-right:0.05em;"><span class="pstrut" style="height:2.7em;"></span><span class="katex-sizing reset-size6 size3 mtight"><span class="mord mathnormal mtight">t</span></span></span></span><span class="vlist-s">​</span></span><span class="vlist-r"><span class="vlist" style="height:0.15em;"><span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span> when members can identify which rules are in force and who is entitled to make, apply and enforce them. Following Hart (1961), the criteria members use for this identification form the collective’s <em>rule of recognition</em>. A belief system supports <em>normative legitimacy</em> when, in addition, members regard the rules or the officials as rightful, so that the reason for compliance includes that judgment and not only the expectation of sanction or the convenience of conformity.</p>
website/out/papers/ideological-power/index.html:26:<p class="thm-head"><span class="thm-label">Definition 2.3</span><span class="thm-name">Legitimating authority</span></p><p>A <em>legitimating authority</em> is an actor whose public statements about <span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>R</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow>R_t</math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="katex-base"><span class="katex-strut" style="height:0.8333em;vertical-align:-0.15em;"></span><span class="mord"><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right:0.0077em;">R</span><span class="msupsub"><span class="vlist-t vlist-t2"><span class="vlist-r"><span class="vlist" style="height:0.2806em;"><span style="top:-2.55em;margin-left:-0.0077em;margin-right:0.05em;"><span class="pstrut" style="height:2.7em;"></span><span class="katex-sizing reset-size6 size3 mtight"><span class="mord mathnormal mtight">t</span></span></span></span><span class="vlist-s">​</span></span><span class="vlist-r"><span class="vlist" style="height:0.15em;"><span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span>, about officials or about facts relevant to compliance move other members’ beliefs, because members expect those statements to track the truth or the tradition rather than the speaker’s interest. website/out/papers/ideological-power/index.html:52:<p class="thm-head"><span class="thm-label">Remark 2.6</span></p><p>.  Common knowledge is an idealization. Rubinstein (1992) showed in the electronic mail game that any finite number of levels of mutual knowledge can fail to support coordination that common knowledge would support. Monderer and Samet (1989) showed that an approximate notion, common <span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow>p</math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="katex-base"><span class="katex-strut" style="height:0.625em;vertical-align:-0.1944em;"></span><span class="mord mathnormal">p</span></span></span></span>-belief, restores continuity: equilibria that require common knowledge are approximated by equilibria under common <span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow>p</math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="katex-base"><span class="katex-strut" style="height:0.625em;vertical-align:-0.1944em;"></span><span class="mord mathnormal">p</span></span></span></span>-belief for <span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow>p</math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="katex-base"><span class="katex-strut" style="height:0.625em;vertical-align:-0.1944em;"></span><span class="mord mathnormal">p</span></span></span></span> close to one. The arguments below go through with public events replaced by events that each member believes with probability at least <span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow>p</math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="katex-base"><span class="katex-strut" style="height:0.625em;vertical-align:-0.1944em;"></span><span class="mord mathnormal">p</span></span></span></span> whenever they occur. class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mn>0</mn><mo separator="true">,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo class="mclose">]</span></span></span></span>, of five components: (i) <em>plurality</em>: the number and audience reach of legitimating authorities whose appointment and funding are independent of one another; (ii) <em>independence</em>: tenure protection, editorial autonomy, academic freedom and juristic or doctrinal autonomy of authorities from the governing coalition; (iii) <em>disclosure</em>: publication of the funding, sponsorship and conflicts of interest of authorities; (iv) <em>reviewability</em>: procedures by which an authority’s statements can be challenged, replicated, corrected or retracted, including peer review, rights of reply and public correction; (v) <em>exit</em>: the ability of audiences to turn to rival authorities without legal or material sanction, the ideological case of exit in the sense of Hirschman (1970), leaving an organization rather than voicing complaint within it, which <a class="xpart" href="/papers/productive-power/">Part VI</a> defines (Definition 2.5 of <a class="xpart" href="/papers/productive-power/#def:productive-power:evl">Part VI</a>).</p>
website/out/papers/ideological-power/index.html:59:<p>The components are not new. They restate the source framework’s contestability for the ideological layer and match the checks it lists for its knowledge mechanism: independent epidemiology, investigative reporting, protected academic freedom and professional resistance (Largo 2026). Their value lies in making the aggregate auditable: each component can be coded from documents, and a disagreement about <span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mi>Q</mi><mi mathvariant="sans-serif">I</mi></msup></mrow>Q^{\mathsf{I}}</math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="katex-base"><span class="katex-strut" style="height:1.0435em;vertical-align:-0.1944em;"></span><span class="mord"><span class="mord mathnormal">Q</span><span class="msupsub"><span class="vlist-t"><span class="vlist-r"><span class="vlist" style="height:0.8491em;"><span style="top:-3.063em;margin-right:0.05em;"><span class="pstrut" style="height:2.7em;"></span><span class="katex-sizing reset-size6 size3 mtight"><span class="mord mtight"><span class="mord mathsf mtight">I</span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span> can be traced to a disagreement about one of them.</p>

A polity whose governing coalition controls every belief-producing institution but none of the other five pillars shows ideological fusion, not system-wide integration. Capture of belief becomes system-wide only through coupling to appointments, budgets or sanctions in other pillars, which is why Section&nbsp;<a class="xref" href="#sec:mechanisms">6</a> studies the couplings.</p>

website/out/papers/ideological-power/index.html:97:<p>The theorem is modest in its mathematics and specific in its content. Its mathematical core is the characterization of common knowledge by public events. Its empirical content sits in the three assumptions, all of which the proof uses, which is where the series’ standard of proof requires it to sit: the necessity claim is derived from stated premises about collective life, and it can fail if the premises fail. <a class="xpart" href="/papers/formalized-state/">Part VII</a> states the general theorem for all six pillars and the non-implication of Proposition B; the present result is the pillar-level piece for <span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi mathvariant="sans-serif">I</mi></mrow>\mathsf{I}</math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="katex-base"><span class="katex-strut" style="height:0.6944em;"></span><span class="mord mathsf">I</span></span></span></span>.</p>

website/out/papers/ideological-power/index.html:149:<p>The Ju/’hoansi are the case most often cited as lacking hierarchy. Their norms of sharing, modesty and restraint are sustained by talk. Wiessner (2005) recorded conversations in Ju/’hoansi camps and found that criticism of norm violations was mostly verbal and directed at behavior such as stinginess and self-aggrandizement. Talk in a small camp has the structure of a public event: speakers and listeners are co-present, and each sees who else hears. Lee (1979) and Lee (2013) describe the custom of deprecating a successful hunter’s kill, which teaches the hunter and everyone listening that boasting will not be tolerated. No one holds an office of teacher or censor. The function is distributed across the whole adult population, so <span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mi>H</mi><mi mathvariant="sans-serif">I</mi></msup></mrow>H^{\mathsf{I}}</math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="katex-base"><span class="katex-strut" style="height:0.8491em;"></span><span class="mord"><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right:0.0813em;">H</span><span class="msupsub"><span class="vlist-t"><span class="vlist-r"><span class="vlist" style="height:0.8491em;"><span style="top:-3.063em;margin-right:0.05em;"><span class="pstrut" style="height:2.7em;"></span><span class="katex-sizing reset-size6 size3 mtight"><span class="mord mtight"><span class="mord mathsf mtight">I</span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span> is close to its minimum and exit to another camp keeps <span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mi>Q</mi><mi mathvariant="sans-serif">I</mi></msup></mrow>Q^{\mathsf{I}}</math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="katex-base"><span class="katex-strut" style="height:1.0435em;vertical-align:-0.1944em;"></span><span class="mord"><span class="mord mathnormal">Q</span><span class="msupsub"><span class="vlist-t"><span class="vlist-r"><span class="vlist" style="height:0.8491em;"><span style="top:-3.063em;margin-right:0.05em;"><span class="pstrut" style="height:2.7em;"></span><span class="katex-sizing reset-size6 size3 mtight"><span class="mord mtight"><span class="mord mathsf mtight">I</span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span> high.</p>
website/out/papers/ideological-power/index.html:157:<p>A second attempt holds that markets coordinate through prices without shared beliefs. Prices do economize on information. But exchange presupposes common knowledge of property conventions: who owns what, what counts as payment, and which contracts are binding. Those conventions are part of <span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>R</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow>R_t</math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="katex-base"><span class="katex-strut" style="height:0.8333em;vertical-align:-0.15em;"></span><span class="mord"><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right:0.0077em;">R</span><span class="msupsub"><span class="vlist-t vlist-t2"><span class="vlist-r"><span class="vlist" style="height:0.2806em;"><span style="top:-2.55em;margin-left:-0.0077em;margin-right:0.05em;"><span class="pstrut" style="height:2.7em;"></span><span class="katex-sizing reset-size6 size3 mtight"><span class="mord mathnormal mtight">t</span></span></span></span><span class="vlist-s">​</span></span><span class="vlist-r"><span class="vlist" style="height:0.15em;"><span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span>, and they are taught, displayed and defended. Hayek (1973) himself stressed that the order of a market society rests on rules of just conduct that people follow without being able to state them; following a rule one cannot state is compatible with common knowledge of the practice it supports.</p>
website/out/papers/ideological-power/index.html:170:<p>Bourdieu (1989), Bourdieu (1991) described symbolic power as the power to constitute the given by stating it, effective to the degree that it is misrecognized as something other than power. His account of the convertibility of economic, cultural and symbolic capital anticipates the cross-pillar coupling <span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="sans-serif">F</mi><mi mathvariant="sans-serif">I</mi></mrow></msub></mrow>C_{\mathsf{F}\mathsf{I}}</math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="katex-base"><span class="katex-strut" style="height:0.8333em;vertical-align:-0.15em;"></span><span class="mord"><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right:0.0715em;">C</span><span class="msupsub"><span class="vlist-t vlist-t2"><span class="vlist-r"><span class="vlist" style="height:0.3361em;"><span style="top:-2.55em;margin-left:-0.0715em;margin-right:0.05em;"><span class="pstrut" style="height:2.7em;"></span><span class="katex-sizing reset-size6 size3 mtight"><span class="mord mtight"><span class="mord mathsf mtight">FI</span></span></span></span></span><span class="vlist-s">​</span></span><span class="vlist-r"><span class="vlist" style="height:0.15em;"><span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span>, which <a class="xpart" href="/papers/financial-power/">Part I</a> treats as its pair. Bourdieu and Passeron (1977) applied the account to schooling, arguing that educational systems reproduce class structure while appearing meritocratic.</p>
website/out/papers/ideological-power/index.html:172:<p>Habermas (1989) traced the rise of a bourgeois public sphere of rational-critical debate in eighteenth-century Europe and its later refeudalization, as mass media and organized interests turned a reasoning public into an audience. Fraser (1990) argued that the bourgeois public sphere excluded women, workers and others, who formed subaltern counterpublics of their own. Both accounts bear on the plurality component of <span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mi>Q</mi><mi mathvariant="sans-serif">I</mi></msup></mrow>Q^{\mathsf{I}}</math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="katex-base"><span class="katex-strut" style="height:1.0435em;vertical-align:-0.1944em;"></span><span class="mord"><span class="mord mathnormal">Q</span><span class="msupsub"><span class="vlist-t"><span class="vlist-r"><span class="vlist" style="height:0.8491em;"><span style="top:-3.063em;margin-right:0.05em;"><span class="pstrut" style="height:2.7em;"></span><span class="katex-sizing reset-size6 size3 mtight"><span class="mord mtight"><span class="mord mathsf mtight">I</span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span>: a public sphere is contestable to the degree that counterpublics can form and be heard.</p>

website/out/papers/ideological-power/index.html:189:<p>In market-capitalist societies the ideological function is held by many organizations with separate ownership and funding: privately owned media firms financed by advertising and subscriptions, public and private universities, foundations and think tanks, professional associations, scientific journals, regulatory agencies in their certifying role, and religious bodies organized as voluntary associations. Control over authoritative outputs is spread across these organizations, so <span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mi>H</mi><mi mathvariant="sans-serif">I</mi></msup></mrow>H^{\mathsf{I}}</math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="katex-base"><span class="katex-strut" style="height:0.8491em;"></span><span class="mord"><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right:0.0813em;">H</span><span class="msupsub"><span class="vlist-t"><span class="vlist-r"><span class="vlist" style="height:0.8491em;"><span style="top:-3.063em;margin-right:0.05em;"><span class="pstrut" style="height:2.7em;"></span><span class="katex-sizing reset-size6 size3 mtight"><span class="mord mtight"><span class="mord mathsf mtight">I</span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span> is moderate overall, but it varies by sector. Ownership of the largest media firms is often concentrated in a few families (Djankov et&nbsp;al. 2003), while accreditation of physicians or approval of drugs may rest with a single professional body or agency.</p>
website/out/papers/ideological-power/index.html:190:<p>The distinctive coupling is between the financial and ideological pillars. Advertising finances news, endowments and grants finance universities, and industry finances a large share of clinical research. Herman and Chomsky (1988) built their propaganda model on this coupling. Slaughter and Rhoades (2004) documented the movement of universities toward market revenue, and Starr (1982) described how medical authority was converted into economic power and later confronted corporate organization of care. <a class="xpart" href="/papers/financial-power/">Part I</a> treats <span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="sans-serif">F</mi><mi mathvariant="sans-serif">I</mi></mrow></msub></mrow>C_{\mathsf{F}\mathsf{I}}</math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="katex-base"><span class="katex-strut" style="height:0.8333em;vertical-align:-0.15em;"></span><span class="mord"><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right:0.0715em;">C</span><span class="msupsub"><span class="vlist-t vlist-t2"><span class="vlist-r"><span class="vlist" style="height:0.3361em;"><span style="top:-2.55em;margin-left:-0.0715em;margin-right:0.05em;"><span class="pstrut" style="height:2.7em;"></span><span class="katex-sizing reset-size6 size3 mtight"><span class="mord mtight"><span class="mord mathsf mtight">FI</span></span></span></span></span><span class="vlist-s">​</span></span><span class="vlist-r"><span class="vlist" style="height:0.15em;"><span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span> as its pair and measures the conversion of financial control into favorable outputs of other pillars by a conversion elasticity (Definition 6.1 of <a class="xpart" href="/papers/financial-power/#def:financial-power:conversion">Part I</a>); here the question is what the coupling does to the independence parameter <span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>λ</mi></mrow>\lambda</math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="katex-base"><span class="katex-strut" style="height:0.6944em;"></span><span class="mord mathnormal">λ</span></span></span></span> of Definition&nbsp;<a class="xref" href="#def:ideological-power:endorsement">6.1</a>.</p>
website/out/papers/ideological-power/index.html:192:<p>Platform firms now hold part of the function in this regime type. A few companies decide, through ranking and moderation, which statements by journalists, scientists and clergy reach large audiences (Gillespie 2019). In the terms of Section&nbsp;<a class="xref" href="#sec:layer">2</a>, they hold a large share of control over reach, one of the outputs that defines <span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mi>s</mi><mi mathvariant="sans-serif">I</mi></msup></mrow>s^{\mathsf{I}}</math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="katex-base"><span class="katex-strut" style="height:0.8491em;"></span><span class="mord"><span class="mord mathnormal">s</span><span class="msupsub"><span class="vlist-t"><span class="vlist-r"><span class="vlist" style="height:0.8491em;"><span style="top:-3.063em;margin-right:0.05em;"><span class="pstrut" style="height:2.7em;"></span><span class="katex-sizing reset-size6 size3 mtight"><span class="mord mtight"><span class="mord mathsf mtight">I</span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span>, so they raise measured concentration even when the number of speakers grows. The evidence on their persuasive effect is mixed: fabricated stories spread widely (Allcott and Gentzkow 2017), but an experimental change of feed ranking during an election left attitudes unchanged (Guess et&nbsp;al. 2023). Control over reach is established; its translation into belief is an open empirical question.</p>
website/out/papers/ideological-power/index.html:193:<p>The documented checks are also sectoral. Competition among outlets makes media capture costly (Besley and Prat 2006). Demand-side slant (Gentzkow and Shapiro 2006) is a rival explanation for partisan coverage that does not require owner control, so evidence of slant is not by itself evidence of capture. Disclosure rules, peer review, replication and the reputational autonomy of regulators (Carpenter 2010) raise <span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi>λ</mi></mrow>\lambda</math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="katex-base"><span class="katex-strut" style="height:0.6944em;"></span><span class="mord mathnormal">λ</span></span></span></span>. The capture episodes above were themselves discovered through litigation, journalism and meta-research, which is what source hypothesis H4 predicts: higher rates of documented error discovery can signal stronger accountability rather than more capture (Largo 2026).</p>
website/out/papers/ideological-power/index.html:196:<p>Concentration is high by design. Appointments of editors, rectors and academy presidents pass through the party’s appointment channel, the map from a coalition to the offices it fills in each pillar (Definition 2.8 of <a class="xpart" href="/papers/political-power/#def:political-power:appointment-channel">Part II</a>), so <span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="sans-serif">P</mi><mi mathvariant="sans-serif">I</mi></mrow></msub></mrow>C_{\mathsf{P}\mathsf{I}}</math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="katex-base"><span class="katex-strut" style="height:0.8333em;vertical-align:-0.15em;"></span><span class="mord"><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right:0.0715em;">C</span><span class="msupsub"><span class="vlist-t vlist-t2"><span class="vlist-r"><span class="vlist" style="height:0.3361em;"><span style="top:-2.55em;margin-left:-0.0715em;margin-right:0.05em;"><span class="pstrut" style="height:2.7em;"></span><span class="katex-sizing reset-size6 size3 mtight"><span class="mord mtight"><span class="mord mathsf mtight">PI</span></span></span></span></span><span class="vlist-s">​</span></span><span class="vlist-r"><span class="vlist" style="height:0.15em;"><span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span> is high and <span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msup><mi>H</mi><mi mathvariant="sans-serif">I</mi></msup></mrow>H^{\mathsf{I}}</math></span><span style="margin-right:0.0813em;">H</span><span class="msupsub"><span class="vlist-t"><span class="vlist-r"><span class="vlist" style="height:0.8491em;"><span style="top:-3.063em;margin-right:0.05em;"><span class="pstrut" style="height:2.7em;"></span><span class="katex-sizing reset-size6 size3 mtight"><span class="mord mtight"><span class="mord mathsf mtight">I</span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span> approaches its maximum in the formal structure. Coupling to the coercive pillar is strong: censorship offices and security services enforce the boundaries of permissible expression, and <a class="xpart" href="/papers/coercive-power/">Part V</a> treats the security services themselves. Althusser (1971)’s concept of ideological state apparatuses, developed within Marxism, describes this configuration more literally than it describes the societies Althusser had in mind.</p>
website/out/papers/ideological-power/index.html:201:<p>Concentration in broadcasting can be high, because a public broadcaster may hold a large audience share. Contestability then depends on the governance of that broadcaster: who appoints its board, how its budget is set, and whether editors are protected. Coupling to the political pillar runs through these appointment and budget channels, and <a class="xpart" href="/papers/political-power/">Part II</a> treats <span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="sans-serif">P</mi><mi mathvariant="sans-serif">I</mi></mrow></msub></mrow>C_{\mathsf{P}\mathsf{I}}</math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="katex-base"><span class="katex-strut" style="height:0.8333em;vertical-align:-0.15em;"></span><span class="mord"><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right:0.0715em;">C</span><span class="msupsub"><span class="vlist-t vlist-t2"><span class="vlist-r"><span class="vlist" style="height:0.3361em;"><span style="top:-2.55em;margin-left:-0.0715em;margin-right:0.05em;"><span class="pstrut" style="height:2.7em;"></span><span class="katex-sizing reset-size6 size3 mtight"><span class="mord mtight"><span class="mord mathsf mtight">PI</span></span></span></span></span><span class="vlist-s">​</span></span><span class="vlist-r"><span class="vlist" style="height:0.15em;"><span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span> as its pair. Coupling to the productive pillar is distinctive in this regime type. Unions and labor parties historically ran newspapers, educational associations and adult education, so the beliefs of the producing population were shaped partly by organizations that the producers themselves controlled. Berman (2006) argued that social democracy’s defining idea was the primacy of politics over markets, an ideological commitment advanced through party organization. Esping-Andersen (1990) argued that universal welfare programs build cross-class support for the welfare state, and Rothstein (1996) analyzed how the Swedish model depended on the administrative implementation of reforms. Universal programs thus have an ideological consequence: they produce shared beliefs about entitlement that sustain the programs themselves.</p>
website/out/papers/ideological-power/index.html:206:<p>Later states increased the coupling. In the Ottoman empire the learned hierarchy was organized as a career of salaried officials under the chief jurist, the Şeyhülislam, and Imber (1997) showed how the chief jurist Ebu’s-su’ud harmonized sultanic law with the sharia; <span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="sans-serif">P</mi><mi mathvariant="sans-serif">I</mi></mrow></msub></mrow>C_{\mathsf{P}\mathsf{I}}</math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="katex-base"><span class="katex-strut" style="height:0.8333em;vertical-align:-0.15em;"></span><span class="mord"><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right:0.0715em;">C</span><span class="msupsub"><span class="vlist-t vlist-t2"><span class="vlist-r"><span class="vlist" style="height:0.3361em;"><span style="top:-2.55em;margin-left:-0.0715em;margin-right:0.05em;"><span class="pstrut" style="height:2.7em;"></span><span class="katex-sizing reset-size6 size3 mtight"><span class="mord mtight"><span class="mord mathsf mtight">PI</span></span></span></span></span><span class="vlist-s">​</span></span><span class="vlist-r"><span class="vlist" style="height:0.15em;"><span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span> was correspondingly high, while Barkey (2008) emphasized the empire’s reliance on brokered intermediaries and its accommodation of diversity. In Saudi Arabia, Commins (2006) and Al-Rasheed (2002) describe an alliance between the ruling dynasty and the Wahhabi religious establishment, in which scholars legitimated the dynasty and received authority over religious education and public morals. In Iran, Arjomand (1988) analyzed how the revolution of 1979 created a clerical state, building on a doctrine of guardianship by the jurist that Khomeini (1981) had set out, and Menashri (1992) traced the relation between education and state ideology in modern Iran. Here the fusion of religious and political authority raises <span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="sans-serif">P</mi><mi mathvariant="sans-serif">I</mi></mrow></msub></mrow>C_{\mathsf{P}\mathsf{I}}</math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="katex-base"><span class="katex-strut" style="height:0.8333em;vertical-align:-0.15em;"></span><span class="mord"><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right:0.0715em;">C</span><span class="msupsub"><span class="vlist-t vlist-t2"><span class="vlist-r"><span class="vlist" style="height:0.3361em;"><span style="top:-2.55em;margin-left:-0.0715em;margin-right:0.05em;"><span class="pstrut" style="height:2.7em;"></span><span class="katex-sizing reset-size6 size3 mtight"><span class="mord mtight"><span class="mord mathsf mtight">PI</span></span></span></span></span><span class="vlist-s">​</span></span><span class="vlist-r"><span class="vlist" style="height:0.15em;"><span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span> and <span class="katex"><span mathvariant="sans-serif">I</mi></mrow></msub></mrow>C_{\mathsf{J}\mathsf{I}}</math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="katex-base"><span class="katex-strut" style="height:0.8333em;vertical-align:-0.15em;"></span><span class="mord"><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right:0.0715em;">C</span><span class="msupsub"><span class="vlist-t vlist-t2"><span class="vlist-r"><span class="vlist" style="height:0.3361em;"><span style="top:-2.55em;margin-left:-0.0715em;margin-right:0.05em;"><span class="pstrut" style="height:2.7em;"></span><span class="katex-sizing reset-size6 size3 mtight"><span class="mord mtight"><span class="mord mathsf mtight">JI</span></span></span></span></span><span class="vlist-s">​</span></span><span class="vlist-r"><span class="vlist" style="height:0.15em;"><span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span> toward their maximum, although the Shia clergy’s older tradition of plural, independently followed authorities remains a source of internal diversity.</p>
website/out/papers/ideological-power/index.html:212:<p>The configuration varied. In the Papal States temporal and spiritual authority were held by the same sovereign, so <span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="sans-serif">P</mi><mi mathvariant="sans-serif">I</mi></mrow></msub></mrow>C_{\mathsf{P}\mathsf{I}}</math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="katex-base"><span class="katex-strut" style="height:0.8333em;vertical-align:-0.15em;"></span><span class="mord"><span class="mord mathnormal" style="margin-right:0.0715em;">C</span><span class="msupsub"><span class="vlist-t vlist-t2"><span class="vlist-r"><span class="vlist" style="height:0.3361em;"><span style="top:-2.55em;margin-left:-0.0715em;margin-right:0.05em;"><span class="pstrut" style="height:2.7em;"></span><span class="katex-sizing reset-size6 size3 mtight"><span class="mord mtight"><span class="mord mathsf mtight">PI</span></span></span></span></span><span class="vlist-s">​</span></span><span class="vlist-r"><span class="vlist" style="height:0.15em;"><span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span></span> reached its maximum. In Habsburg Spain the Inquisition operated under royal as well as papal authority and coupled the ideological pillar to the judicial and coercive pillars. Kamen (1997) argued that the Inquisition’s scale and severity were smaller than the black legend held and that it served local and royal interests as much as doctrinal ones; that revision is itself debated, and the quantitative studies of trial records collected by Henningsen and Tedeschi (1986) supply the evidence on which the debate turns. In Bourbon France, Burke (1992) showed how the image of Louis XIV was manufactured by artists, writers and academies working for the crown, and Bossuet (1990) supplied the scriptural theory of divine-right monarchy. Kantorowicz (1957) traced the older political theology of the king’s two bodies on which such theories drew.</p>

website/out/papers/ideological-power/index.html:296:<p>A governing coalition values public confidence in its rules and also values control over authorities for its own sake, because control lets it direct authoritative outputs toward other ends. Independence is largely fixed in advance, by charters, endowments, tenure rules and appointment procedures, before the coalition knows whether the rules it will later need endorsed are sound. website/out/papers/ideological-power/index.html:312:<p>The proposition is a conditional comparative static, and its key parameter is alignment. A coalition values independent authorities only when it gains more from public confidence in sound rules than in unsound ones (<span class="katex"><span class="katex-mathml"><math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo>&gt;</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow>\Delta&gt;0</math></span><span class="katex-html" aria-hidden="true"><span class="katex-base"><span class="katex-strut" style="height:0.7224em;vertical-align:-0.0391em;"></span><span class="mord">Δ</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right:0.2778em;"></span><span class="mrel">&gt;</span><span class="mspace" style="margin-right:0.2778em;"></span></span><span class="katex-base"><span class="katex-strut" style="height:0.6444em;"></span><span class="mord">0</span></span></span></span>), which is the case when its interests run with the public’s: a government that wants a vaccine taken because it works, not because a contract depends on it. out/papers/coercive-power/index.html
meta {"og:title":"Coercive Power and Enforcement","og:description":"Every governance system must decide who enforces its rules. This paper derives the coercive function from one axiom, that members sometimes have reason to break rules, and compares how six regime types distribute it. A deterrence theorem shows that when the share of agents tempted to violate a rule exceeds the violation rate the collective can tolerate, compliance requires that violators’ continuation payoffs fall because of their own conduct. A sanction regime of some kind is therefore necessary, but no particular institution is. Gossip, ostracism and coalition action against would-be dominants meet this requirement as well as police do, as the ethnography of the Nuer, the Ju/’hoansi, Amazonian societies and Ostrom’s commons documents. A second result shows why, where sanctions are costly public goods and higher-order sanctions are absent, coercion at scale depends on provisioning or on shared norms of punishment. The paper then separates two properties of any enforcement apparatus: its conduct margin, how much more likely a violator is to be sanctioned than a complier, and its allegiance margin, how much more likely an opponent is to be sanctioned than a supporter. The two margins vary independently, so the necessity of coercion does not imply its capture. When capacity is limited, allegiance targeting weakens deterrence for at least one group; when opponents are targeted regardless of conduct, it also raises the volume of coercion against them, so spending and arrest counts mismeasure coercive power. The main limitation is that neither margin has yet been estimated.","og:url":"https://the-beast-system.vercel.app/papers/coercive-power/","og:image":"https://the-beast-system.vercel.app/og/coercive-power.png","og:image:width":"1200","og:image:height":"630","og:type":"article","twitter:card":"summary_large_image","twitter:title":"Coercive Power and Enforcement","twitter:description":"Every governance system must decide who enforces its rules. A second result shows why, where sanctions are costly public goods and higher-order sanctions are absent, coercion at scale depends on provisioning or on shared norms of punishment. The paper then separates two properties of any enforcement apparatus: its conduct margin, how much more likely a violator is to be sanctioned than a complier, and its allegiance margin, how much more likely an opponent is to be sanctioned than a supporter. The two margins vary independently, so the necessity of coercion does not imply its capture. When capacity is limited, allegiance targeting weakens deterrence for at least one group; when opponents are targeted regardless of conduct, it also raises the volume of coercion against them, so spending and arrest counts mismeasure coercive power. out/papers/financial-power/index.html
meta {"og:title":"Financial Power and Resource Command","og:description":"Every governance system must settle conflicting claims on finite resources. This paper treats that settlement as the financial pillar of a six-function model of governance and asks who controls resources across regime types. From a scarcity axiom and an explicit assumption that unsettled conflicts carry a positive hazard of dissolution, we prove that a collective with no recognized allocation regularity cannot persist with probability bounded away from zero, and that in any collective that does persist the share of conflicts settled by such a regularity tends to one. The result concerns a function, not an institution: in foraging bands the regularity is a sharing norm, and control is dispersed close to the minimum concentration the index allows. We then prove that the necessity of the pillar places no restriction on its concentration or contestability, show that aggregating subdomains understates concentration by exactly the cross-domain variance of control shares, and derive conditional comparative statics under which resource holders convert wealth into influence over rules. A comparison of market-capitalist societies, communist party-states, social democracies, Islamic states, Catholic monarchies and secular democracies finds the same function held by different institutions, with documented capture episodes and documented checks in every type. Seven hypotheses with stated falsifiers make the capture claim testable. Revelation 13 and 18 are read typologically as images of economic participation conditioned on allegiance. The main limitation is that no coded cross-regime dataset yet exists, so the comparative claims remain qualitative.","og:url":"https://the-beast-system.vercel.app/papers/financial-power/","og:image":"https://the-beast-system.vercel.app/og/financial-power.png","og:image:width":"1200","og:image:height":"630","og:type":"article","twitter:card":"summary_large_image","twitter:title":"Financial Power and Resource Command","twitter:description":"Every governance system must settle conflicting claims on finite resources. The result concerns a function, not an institution: in foraging bands the regularity is a sharing norm, and control is dispersed close to the minimum concentration the index allows. We then prove that the necessity of the pillar places no restriction on its concentration or contestability, show that aggregating subdomains understates concentration by exactly the cross-domain variance of control shares, and derive conditional comparative statics under which resource holders convert wealth into influence over rules. A comparison of market-capitalist societies, communist party-states, social democracies, Islamic states, Catholic monarchies and secular democracies finds the same function held by different institutions, with documented capture episodes and documented checks in every type. Seven hypotheses with stated falsifiers make the capture claim testable. Revelation 13 and 18 are read typologically as images of economic participation conditioned on allegiance. The main limitation is that no coded cross-regime dataset yet exists, so the comparative claims remain qualitative.","twitter:image":"https://the-beast-system.vercel.app/og/financial-power.png"}

out/papers/formalized-state/index.html
meta {"og:title":"The Formalized State: The Hierarchy of the Beast System","og:description":"Every governance system must decide who controls resources, who makes and interprets rules, who shapes beliefs, who enforces and who produces. This paper defines the Formalized State, a class of structures with six layers of control, a role map and a dependency hypergraph, and proves four results relative to stated axioms and a stated set of preserved properties: roles, control shares, concentration, contestability, integration and dependencies. Representation: every governance system satisfying the axioms is equivalent to a Formalized State structure, while content, ideology and procedure are forgotten. Necessity: six axioms about collective life (scarcity, plurality, generality, coordination, defection and maintenance) force the six functions, each axiom can fail in a persistent model, and four incidence axioms with falsifiers make the functions fully interdependent, although interpretation needs legitimation or coercion rather than both. Minimality: dropping or merging any pillar identifies systems that differ in a preserved property, with explicit witness pairs. Uniqueness: the abstraction is the coarsest one preserving those properties, unique up to unique isomorphism, with exactly six dimensions. Encodings of Aristotle, Weber, Parsons, Easton, Almond, Luhmann and Mann each identify two systems the abstraction distinguishes, so none is equivalent to it. Capture is a property of instances: structures satisfying every axiom occupy all four corners of the concentration and integration square, and a conversion model shows when capture becomes irreversible. No real polity has yet been coded.","og:url":"https://the-beast-system.vercel.app/papers/formalized-state/","og:image":"https://the-beast-system.vercel.app/og/formalized-state.png","og:image:width":"1200","og:image:height":"630","og:type":"article","twitter:card":"summary_large_image","twitter:title":"The Formalized State: The Hierarchy of the Beast System","twitter:description":"Every governance system must decide who controls resources, who makes and interprets rules, who shapes beliefs, who enforces and who produces. Minimality: dropping or merging any pillar identifies systems that differ in a preserved property, with explicit witness pairs. Uniqueness: the abstraction is the coarsest one preserving those properties, unique up to unique isomorphism, with exactly six dimensions. Encodings of Aristotle, Weber, Parsons, Easton, Almond, Luhmann and Mann each identify two systems the abstraction distinguishes, so none is equivalent to it. out/papers/ideological-power/index.html
meta {"og:title":"Ideological Power and Legitimation","og:description":"Every governance system must settle who shapes the beliefs on which cooperation depends. This paper treats that question as the ideological pillar of a six-pillar model of governance and asks two things of it: whether the pillar is necessary, and when it becomes an instrument of capture. From a coordination axiom, together with membership turnover and the cross-cultural variability of rules, we derive that every persistent collective implements a recognition function: a recurring public practice that makes the operative rules common knowledge. The derivation establishes the necessity of a function, not of any institution, and it does not establish that belief in the rightness of rules is necessary. Stateless and egalitarian societies implement the function through talk, ridicule, ritual and kinship idiom, without a designated office. A Bayesian endorsement model then shows that a captured authority’s endorsement carries no information, that independent authorities raise expected public confidence in sound rules and lower it for unsound ones, and that coordinated control of several authorities lowers the probability that an error is disclosed below the level reached by independent control with the same average independence. We compare how academia, religious institutions, media, schools and medical and scientific bodies hold the function in market-capitalist, communist party-state, social-democratic, Islamic, Catholic-monarchical and secular-democratic regimes, and we state hypotheses with falsifiers. The comparative codings are qualitative and drawn from secondary literature; no concentration or integration index is estimated for any real polity.","og:url":"https://the-beast-system.vercel.app/papers/ideological-power/","og:image":"https://the-beast-system.vercel.app/og/ideological-power.png","og:image:width":"1200","og:image:height":"630","og:type":"article","twitter:card":"summary_large_image","twitter:title":"Ideological Power and Legitimation","twitter:description":"Every governance system must settle who shapes the beliefs on which cooperation depends. We compare how academia, religious institutions, media, schools and medical and scientific bodies hold the function in market-capitalist, communist party-state, social-democratic, Islamic, Catholic-monarchical and secular-democratic regimes, and we state hypotheses with falsifiers. out/papers/judicial-power/index.html
meta {"og:title":"Judicial Power and Legal Interpretation","og:description":"Every governance system must decide who interprets its laws. General rules cannot settle particular disputes by themselves, because every rule admits more than one reasonable reading at its edges. This paper derives the judicial function from that fact. Under three explicit assumptions (open texture produces disputes that the parties cannot settle alone, self-help is costly to the collective, and exit is costly), any collective that persists indefinitely resolves all but finitely many such disputes through a determination procedure that neither party controls. The derivation requires a function, not an office. Leopard-skin chiefs, Barotse moots, Ju/’hoansi talking-out, qadi courts, the Parlement of Paris and modern constitutional courts all perform it. Two results narrow the claim. When exit is costless the forcing argument fails, which matches the thin adjudication of immediate-return foragers. When rules are executed by code, interpretation relocates to the classification of inputs instead of disappearing. The paper then operationalizes judicial contestability as a chain of disclosure, access, independence and compliance by the powerful, and proves that the probability that a captured ruling persists depends on the product of these links. An additive index can therefore score a judiciary well while a single broken link leaves capture unchecked. A comparison of six regime types, from market capitalism to historical Catholic monarchies, finds the function everywhere and finds wide variation in its concentration and coupling to other pillars. Eight hypotheses with stated falsifiers make the capture claims testable. No numerical concentration scores are reported for real cases.","og:url":"https://the-beast-system.vercel.app/papers/judicial-power/","og:image":"https://the-beast-system.vercel.app/og/judicial-power.png","og:image:width":"1200","og:image:height":"630","og:type":"article","twitter:card":"summary_large_image","twitter:title":"Judicial Power and Legal Interpretation","twitter:description":"Every governance system must decide who interprets its laws. The paper then operationalizes judicial contestability as a chain of disclosure, access, independence and compliance by the powerful, and proves that the probability that a captured ruling persists depends on the product of these links. An additive index can therefore score a judiciary well while a single broken link leaves capture unchecked. out/papers/political-power/index.html
meta {"og:title":"Political Power and Rule Making","og:description":"Every governance system must settle who makes the rules. This paper treats rule making as one pillar of a six-function model of governance and separates two questions about it: whether the function is necessary, and how its control is distributed. From an axiom of plurality (members’ preferences diverge, yet some choices bind everyone), together with environmental change and the persistence of the group, we prove that every persistent collective implements a rule-making function, though not any particular institution. In stateless and consensus societies the function appears as camp discussion, lineage moots, oratory without command, and fission. We measure the distribution of rule-making power with power indices over decision procedures and prove that necessity places no constraint on concentration: for a group of n members and every k from 1 to n, some procedure satisfies the necessity lemma with concentration exactly 1/k. Three conditional propositions describe how rule making can turn into capture: monitoring incentives that vanish as organizations grow, veto structures that protect preferential status quo rules, and appointment channels that couple rule making to courts, security services, and the economy. We compare market capitalism, communist party-states, social democracy, Islamic states, Catholic monarchies, and secular democracies on identical questions, state seven hypotheses with falsifiers, and read Revelation 13 and 17 typologically as an image of rule-making authority that admits no contest. The main limitation is that no regime is coded numerically; the comparative claims are qualitative and await preregistered measurement.","og:url":"https://the-beast-system.vercel.app/papers/political-power/","og:image":"https://the-beast-system.vercel.app/og/political-power.png","og:image:width":"1200","og:image:height":"630","og:type":"article","twitter:card":"summary_large_image","twitter:title":"Political Power and Rule Making","twitter:description":"Every governance system must settle who makes the rules. In stateless and consensus societies the function appears as camp discussion, lineage moots, oratory without command, and fission. We measure the distribution of rule-making power with power indices over decision procedures and prove that necessity places no constraint on concentration: for a group of n members and every k from 1 to n, some procedure satisfies the necessity lemma with concentration exactly 1/k. Three conditional propositions describe how rule making can turn into capture: monitoring incentives that vanish as organizations grow, veto structures that protect preferential status quo rules, and appointment channels that couple rule making to courts, security services, and the economy. We compare market capitalism, communist party-states, social democracy, Islamic states, Catholic monarchies, and secular democracies on identical questions, state seven hypotheses with falsifiers, and read Revelation 13 and 17 typologically as an image of rule-making authority that admits no contest. The main limitation is that no regime is coded numerically; the comparative claims are qualitative and await preregistered measurement.","twitter:image":"https://the-beast-system.vercel.app/og/political-power.png"}

out/papers/productive-power/index.html
meta {"og:title":"Productive Power and Social Reproduction","og:description":"Every governance system consumes resources that someone must produce. This paper treats production, payment and social reproduction as the sixth pillar of a comparative framework in which six functions (resource allocation, rule-making, adjudication, legitimation, sanction and production) are present in every functioning polity. From a maintenance axiom we prove that a persistent collective must produce at a positive average rate and must reproduce its producers through care labor, and that rents, tribute, migration or automation relocate production rather than remove it. The same dependence gives producers a latent veto: when outside revenue falls short of the institutions’ maintenance requirement, a collective withdrawal of labor, taxes or trade threatens their persistence. A bargaining model makes the channels exact. Producers’ terms rise with their outside option and organized bargaining weight, fall linearly with the concentration of control over productive participation, and lose their withdrawal premium once rents cover the maintenance requirement. Restricting mobility pays only when the value of free exit exceeds the cost of enforcement, a condition that nests Domar’s land-labor hypothesis and Brenner’s emphasis on class organization. Every instrument that depresses producers’ terms is held in another pillar, so the capture of production never originates inside it. A comparison of six regime types finds the function everywhere and its capture only under specific couplings. Read typologically, Revelation 13:16 and 17 depict the limiting case in which exchange is conditioned on allegiance. The parameters are not estimated here; nine hypotheses state what would falsify the model.","og:url":"https://the-beast-system.vercel.app/papers/productive-power/","og:image":"https://the-beast-system.vercel.app/og/productive-power.png","og:image:width":"1200","og:image:height":"630","og:type":"article","twitter:card":"summary_large_image","twitter:title":"Productive Power and Social Reproduction","twitter:description":"Every governance system consumes resources that someone must produce. A bargaining model makes the channels exact. Restricting mobility pays only when the value of free exit exceeds the cost of enforcement, a condition that nests Domar’s land-labor hypothesis and Brenner’s emphasis on class organization. Every instrument that depresses producers’ terms is held in another pillar, so the capture of production never originates inside it. website/out/index.html:1:<meta property="og:title" content="The Six Pillars of the Beast System"
website/out/index.html:1:<meta property="og:description" content="The six-pillar framework identifies an invariant structure of human governance, supported by historical observation and given precise expression through mathematics."

website/out/papers/financial-power/index.html:1:<meta property="og:title" content="Financial Power and Resource Command"
website/out/papers/financial-power/index.html:1:<meta property="og:description" content="Every governance system must settle conflicting claims on finite resources. This paper treats that settlement as the financial pillar of a six-function model of governance and asks who controls resources across regime types. From a scarcity axiom and an explicit assumption that unsettled conflicts carry a positive hazard of dissolution, we prove that a collective with no recognized allocation regularity cannot persist with probability bounded away from zero, and that in any collective that does persist the share of conflicts settled by such a regularity tends to one. The result concerns a function, not an institution: in foraging bands the regularity is a sharing norm, and control is dispersed close to the minimum concentration the index allows. We then prove that the necessity of the pillar places no restriction on its concentration or contestability, show that aggregating subdomains understates concentration by exactly the cross-domain variance of control shares, and derive conditional comparative statics under which resource holders convert wealth into influence over rules. A comparison of market-capitalist societies, communist party-states, social democracies, Islamic states, Catholic monarchies and secular democracies finds the same function held by different institutions, with documented capture episodes and documented checks in every type. Seven hypotheses with stated falsifiers make the capture claim testable. Revelation 13 and 18 are read typologically as images of economic participation conditioned on allegiance. The main limitation is that no coded cross-regime dataset yet exists, so the comparative claims remain qualitative."

The result concerns a function, not an institution: in foraging bands the regularity is a sharing norm, and control is dispersed close to the minimum concentration the index allows. We then prove that the necessity of the pillar places no restriction on its concentration or contestability, show that aggregating subdomains understates concentration by exactly the cross-domain variance of control shares, and derive conditional comparative statics under which resource holders convert wealth into influence over rules. A comparison of market-capitalist societies, communist party-states, social democracies, Islamic states, Catholic monarchies and secular democracies finds the same function held by different institutions, with documented capture episodes and documented checks in every type. Seven hypotheses with stated falsifiers make the capture claim testable. Revelation 13 and 18 are read typologically as images of economic participation conditioned on allegiance. The main limitation is that no coded cross-regime dataset yet exists, so the comparative claims remain qualitative."

website/out/papers/judicial-power/index.html:1:<meta property="og:title" content="Judicial Power and Legal Interpretation"
website/out/papers/judicial-power/index.html:1:<meta property="og:description" content="Every governance system must decide who interprets its laws. General rules cannot settle particular disputes by themselves, because every rule admits more than one reasonable reading at its edges. This paper derives the judicial function from that fact. Under three explicit assumptions (open texture produces disputes that the parties cannot settle alone, self-help is costly to the collective, and exit is costly), any collective that persists indefinitely resolves all but finitely many such disputes through a determination procedure that neither party controls. The derivation requires a function, not an office. Leopard-skin chiefs, Barotse moots, Ju/’hoansi talking-out, qadi courts, the Parlement of Paris and modern constitutional courts all perform it. Two results narrow the claim. When exit is costless the forcing argument fails, which matches the thin adjudication of immediate-return foragers. When rules are executed by code, interpretation relocates to the classification of inputs instead of disappearing. The paper then operationalizes judicial contestability as a chain of disclosure, access, independence and compliance by the powerful, and proves that the probability that a captured ruling persists depends on the product of these links. An additive index can therefore score a judiciary well while a single broken link leaves capture unchecked. A comparison of six regime types, from market capitalism to historical Catholic monarchies, finds the function everywhere and finds wide variation in its concentration and coupling to other pillars. Eight hypotheses with stated falsifiers make the capture claims testable. No numerical concentration scores are reported for real cases."

website/out/papers/judicial-power/index.html:1:<meta name="twitter:description" content="Every governance system must decide who interprets its laws. General rules cannot settle particular disputes by themselves, because every rule admits more than one reasonable reading at its edges. This paper derives the judicial function from that fact. Under three explicit assumptions (open texture produces disputes that the parties cannot settle alone, self-help is costly to the collective, and exit is costly), any collective that persists indefinitely resolves all but finitely many such disputes through a determination procedure that neither party controls. The derivation requires a function, not an office. Leopard-skin chiefs, Barotse moots, Ju/’hoansi talking-out, qadi courts, the Parlement of Paris and modern constitutional courts all perform it. Two results narrow the claim. When exit is costless the forcing argument fails, which matches the thin adjudication of immediate-return foragers. When rules are executed by code, interpretation relocates to the classification of inputs instead of disappearing. The paper then operationalizes judicial contestability as a chain of disclosure, access, independence and compliance by the powerful, and proves that the probability that a captured ruling persists depends on the product of these links. An additive index can therefore score a judiciary well while a single broken link leaves capture unchecked. A comparison of six regime types, from market capitalism to historical Catholic monarchies, finds the function everywhere and finds wide variation in its concentration and coupling to other pillars. Eight hypotheses with stated falsifiers make the capture claims testable. No numerical concentration scores are reported for real cases."

website/out/papers/political-power/index.html:1:<meta property="og:title" content="Political Power and Rule Making"
website/out/papers/political-power/index.html:1:<meta property="og:description" content="Every governance system must settle who makes the rules. This paper treats rule making as one pillar of a six-function model of governance and separates two questions about it: whether the function is necessary, and how its control is distributed. From an axiom of plurality (members’ preferences diverge, yet some choices bind everyone), together with environmental change and the persistence of the group, we prove that every persistent collective implements a rule-making function, though not any particular institution. In stateless and consensus societies the function appears as camp discussion, lineage moots, oratory without command, and fission. We measure the distribution of rule-making power with power indices over decision procedures and prove that necessity places no constraint on concentration: for a group of n members and every k from 1 to n, some procedure satisfies the necessity lemma with concentration exactly 1/k. Three conditional propositions describe how rule making can turn into capture: monitoring incentives that vanish as organizations grow, veto structures that protect preferential status quo rules, and appointment channels that couple rule making to courts, security services, and the economy. We compare market capitalism, communist party-states, social democracy, Islamic states, Catholic monarchies, and secular democracies on identical questions, state seven hypotheses with falsifiers, and read Revelation 13 and 17 typologically as an image of rule-making authority that admits no contest. The main limitation is that no regime is coded numerically; the comparative claims are qualitative and await preregistered measurement."

website/out/papers/political-power/index.html:1:<meta name="twitter:description" content="Every governance system must settle who makes the rules. This paper treats rule making as one pillar of a six-function model of governance and separates two questions about it: whether the function is necessary, and how its control is distributed. From an axiom of plurality (members’ preferences diverge, yet some choices bind everyone), together with environmental change and the persistence of the group, we prove that every persistent collective implements a rule-making function, though not any particular institution. In stateless and consensus societies the function appears as camp discussion, lineage moots, oratory without command, and fission. We measure the distribution of rule-making power with power indices over decision procedures and prove that necessity places no constraint on concentration: for a group of n members and every k from 1 to n, some procedure satisfies the necessity lemma with concentration exactly 1/k. Three conditional propositions describe how rule making can turn into capture: monitoring incentives that vanish as organizations grow, veto structures that protect preferential status quo rules, and appointment channels that couple rule making to courts, security services, and the economy. We compare market capitalism, communist party-states, social democracy, Islamic states, Catholic monarchies, and secular democracies on identical questions, state seven hypotheses with falsifiers, and read Revelation 13 and 17 typologically as an image of rule-making authority that admits no contest. The main limitation is that no regime is coded numerically; the comparative claims are qualitative and await preregistered measurement."

website/out/papers/ideological-power/index.html:1:<meta property="og:title" content="Ideological Power and Legitimation"
website/out/papers/ideological-power/index.html:1:<meta property="og:description" content="Every governance system must settle who shapes the beliefs on which cooperation depends. This paper treats that question as the ideological pillar of a six-pillar model of governance and asks two things of it: whether the pillar is necessary, and when it becomes an instrument of capture. From a coordination axiom, together with membership turnover and the cross-cultural variability of rules, we derive that every persistent collective implements a recognition function: a recurring public practice that makes the operative rules common knowledge. The derivation establishes the necessity of a function, not of any institution, and it does not establish that belief in the rightness of rules is necessary. Stateless and egalitarian societies implement the function through talk, ridicule, ritual and kinship idiom, without a designated office. A Bayesian endorsement model then shows that a captured authority’s endorsement carries no information, that independent authorities raise expected public confidence in sound rules and lower it for unsound ones, and that coordinated control of several authorities lowers the probability that an error is disclosed below the level reached by independent control with the same average independence. We compare how academia, religious institutions, media, schools and medical and scientific bodies hold the function in market-capitalist, communist party-state, social-democratic, Islamic, Catholic-monarchical and secular-democratic regimes, and we state hypotheses with falsifiers. The comparative codings are qualitative and drawn from secondary literature; no concentration or integration index is estimated for any real polity."

website/out/papers/ideological-power/index.html:1:<meta name="twitter:description" content="Every governance system must settle who shapes the beliefs on which cooperation depends. This paper treats that question as the ideological pillar of a six-pillar model of governance and asks two things of it: whether the pillar is necessary, and when it becomes an instrument of capture. From a coordination axiom, together with membership turnover and the cross-cultural variability of rules, we derive that every persistent collective implements a recognition function: a recurring public practice that makes the operative rules common knowledge. The derivation establishes the necessity of a function, not of any institution, and it does not establish that belief in the rightness of rules is necessary. Stateless and egalitarian societies implement the function through talk, ridicule, ritual and kinship idiom, without a designated office. A Bayesian endorsement model then shows that a captured authority’s endorsement carries no information, that independent authorities raise expected public confidence in sound rules and lower it for unsound ones, and that coordinated control of several authorities lowers the probability that an error is disclosed below the level reached by independent control with the same average independence. We compare how academia, religious institutions, media, schools and medical and scientific bodies hold the function in market-capitalist, communist party-state, social-democratic, Islamic, Catholic-monarchical and secular-democratic regimes, and we state hypotheses with falsifiers. The comparative codings are qualitative and drawn from secondary literature; no concentration or integration index is estimated for any real polity."
